rw-m1-22.method: Contrast signal 'Far from X' → blank is roughly not-X / opposite of settling.

rw-m1-23.stem:
A student is writing a paragraph about night-sky ordinances and takes these notes:
• Town Q banned most upward-facing outdoor lights in 2016.
• Amateur astronomers reported a 30% increase in visible stars by 2019.
• Energy use for street lighting fell 18% in the same period.
• Neighboring Town R has no lighting ordinance.
• Town R saw no comparable change in either metric.

The student wants to show that Town Q's ordinance likely had multiple benefits. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.C: After Town Q's 2016 ordinance, visible stars rose 30% and street-lighting energy use fell 18%, changes not seen in Town R.
choices.A: Town Q banned upward-facing lights in 2016, while Town R still has no lighting ordinance.
choices.B: Amateur astronomers in Town Q reported seeing more stars by 2019.
choices.D: Town R uses more energy for street lighting than Town Q does.

rw-m1-23.explanation: Multiple benefits = stars + energy, with R as a rough control. B includes both outcomes. A only contrasts policy; C is one benefit; D invents an unsupported comparison.
rw-m1-23.method: Goal = multiple benefits → need at least two positive outcomes tied to the ordinance.
rw-m1-23.speedTip: Count how many claimed benefits the choice actually delivers.
rw-m1-23.commonTrap: A policy contrast that never states benefits.

rw-m1-24.stem:
When a bakery switched from plastic clamshells to compostable boxes, online reviews mentioning packaging jumped from 4% to 22% of all reviews; most of those new mentions were positive. Sales volume was unchanged over the next quarter.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.D: customers noticed and largely approved of the packaging change even though it did not immediately alter how much they bought.
choices.A: compostable boxes caused a sharp decline in overall customer satisfaction.
choices.B: sales would have fallen if the bakery had kept plastic packaging.
choices.C: online reviews became less reliable after the packaging change.

rw-m1-24.explanation: More packaging mentions, mostly positive, with flat sales → awareness/approval without short-term sales shift. B contradicts positive mentions; the other options are unsupported.
rw-m1-24.method: Combine both data points (sentiment and sales) in one cautious inference.
rw-m1-24.speedTip: If sales are flat, do not infer a sales boom or crash.
rw-m1-24.commonTrap: Assuming positive reviews must mean higher sales.

rw-m1-25.stem:
The following text is adapted from a scientist's popular article.

Call the deep ocean empty if you like, but the label is a confession of ignorance. Every remotely operated dive returns footage of organisms that rearrange our maps of where life can persist.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that deep-ocean exploration continually overturns the idea that those waters are barren.
choices.B: To summarize a single remotely operated dive in chronological order.
choices.C: To criticize the funding priorities of marine laboratories.
choices.D: To explain how remotely operated vehicles are built.

rw-m1-25.explanation: The text challenges 'empty' as ignorance and cites dives that revise where life persists — purpose A. It is not a chronological dive report, a funding critique, or an engineering how-to.
rw-m1-25.method: Main purpose = author's primary aim across the whole passage, not a detail.
rw-m1-25.speedTip: Purpose ≠ topic list; pick the verb that matches the author's move (argue, challenge, describe).
rw-m1-25.commonTrap: Choosing a how-to/engineering purpose because ROVs are mentioned.

rw-m1-26.stem:
Historian Ellis Kane contends that nineteenth-century railway timetables did more than coordinate trains: they standardized how ordinary people thought about punctuality in daily life.

Which quotation from a primary source would best support Kane's contention?

choices.A: "The new bridge cut the journey between the two towns from four hours to one."
choices.B: "Since the timetable was posted, factory supervisors dock workers a half day's wage for arriving even ten minutes late."
choices.C: "Locomotive engines required frequent maintenance after long hauls."
choices.D: "Ticket prices fell after competing lines opened in 1871."

rw-m1-26.explanation: Kane's claim is about everyday punctuality norms spreading from railway time. B shows workplaces enforcing minute-level lateness after timetables appeared. A, C, and D concern travel time, maintenance, or prices—not cultural standardization of punctuality.
rw-m1-26.method: Support must hit the specific claim (cultural punctuality), not merely railways.
rw-m1-26.speedTip: Underline the non-obvious part of the claim — here, 'thought about punctuality.'
rw-m1-26.commonTrap: Any railway-related quote that never addresses time discipline in daily life.

rw-m1-27.stem:
The orchestra's guest conductor, ______ insisted on an extra rehearsal before the premiere.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.C: an exacting interpreter of contemporary scores,
choices.A: an exacting interpreter of contemporary scores
choices.B: an exacting interpreter of contemporary scores;
choices.D: she was an exacting interpreter of contemporary scores,

rw-m1-27.explanation: The appositive renaming 'guest conductor' must be set off with commas on both sides; the comma after 'scores' closes the appositive before the verb 'insisted.' A leaves it unclosed; C misuses a semicolon; D creates a comma splice.
rw-m1-27.method: Nonessential appositives: comma before and after.
rw-m1-27.speedTip: If you can lift the phrase out and the sentence still works, wrap it in commas.
rw-m1-27.commonTrap: Omitting the closing comma of the appositive.

math-data-01.stem: The test scores for five students are 72, 85, 90, 68, and 85. What is the mean of these scores?
math-data-01.method: Add all values and divide by the count.
math-data-01.commonTrap: Reporting the mode 85 instead of the mean.

math-data-02.stem: For the data set 72, 85, 90, 68, 85, which statement is true?
math-data-02.explanation: Ordered: 68, 72, 85, 85, 90. Median is the middle value 85. Mode is the most frequent value 85.
math-data-02.method: Sort, then read the middle (median) and the most frequent (mode).
math-data-02.speedTip: With an odd count, the median is simply the center entry after sorting.
math-data-02.commonTrap: Using the unsorted list’s middle entry as the median.

math-data-03.stem: The mean of the numbers 4, 7, 9, 12, and x is 10. What is the value of x?
math-data-03.explanation: Sum of five numbers is 5·10=50. Then 4+7+9+12+x=50 → 32+x=50 → x=18.
math-data-03.method: Use (sum)=mean·n, then isolate the missing value.
math-data-03.commonTrap: Averaging only the four known numbers.

math-data-04.stem: Set A is {10,10,10,10} and set B is {1,5,10,15,19}. Which statement about their standard deviations is true?

choices.A: Set A has the greater standard deviation.
choices.B: Set B has the greater standard deviation.

math-data-04.explanation: Set A has no spread (every value is 10), so SD=0. Set B is widely spread about its center, so its SD is larger.
math-data-04.method: Compare spreads qualitatively: identical values → SD 0; more dispersed values → larger SD.
math-data-04.speedTip: No calculation needed—zero spread vs clear spread.
math-data-04.commonTrap: Thinking the larger mean automatically means larger SD.

math-data-05.stem: A survey of drink preference is shown: Students — tea 40, coffee 60; Teachers — tea 25, coffee 15. What is the probability that a randomly selected tea drinker is a teacher?
math-data-05.explanation: Tea drinkers total 40+25=65. Among them, 25 are teachers. So P(teacher|tea)=25/65.
math-data-05.method: Restrict to the conditioned group (tea), then form the favorable/total ratio.
math-data-05.speedTip: Conditional probability uses only the tea column/row total as the denominator.
math-data-05.commonTrap: Using the grand total 140 instead of the tea total 65.

math-data-06.stem: In a group of 200 people, 120 own a car, 80 own a bike, and 50 own both. How many own neither a car nor a bike?
math-data-06.method: Use inclusion-exclusion, then subtract from the population.
math-data-06.commonTrap: Forgetting to subtract the overlap and computing 200−200=0.

math-data-07.stem: Using the drink table: Students — tea 40, coffee 60; Teachers — tea 25, coffee 15. Given that a person is a student, what is the probability the person prefers coffee?
math-data-07.explanation: There are 100 students; 60 prefer coffee. P(coffee|student)=60/100.
math-data-07.method: Condition on students only; divide coffee-students by all students.
math-data-07.speedTip: Student row total is the denominator.
math-data-07.commonTrap: Dividing by the coffee total or the grand total.

math-data-08.stem: A line of best fit is ŷ=2.5x+10. For x=8, the actual y-value is 28. What is the residual?
math-data-08.method: Compute ŷ from the line, then residual = y−ŷ.
math-data-08.speedTip: Residual negative means the point is below the line.
math-data-08.commonTrap: Reporting predicted−actual with the wrong sign.

math-data-09.stem: The sum of 8 test scores is 640. What is the mean of the scores?
math-data-09.commonTrap: Dividing by 7 or 9 after a fence-post error.

math-data-10.stem: A researcher wants to estimate how often adults in a city exercise. The researcher surveys only people leaving a gym at noon. Which statement best describes this sampling method?

choices.A: It is likely unbiased because noon is a typical time.
choices.B: It is biased toward people who already exercise.
choices.C: It is a simple random sample of the city.
choices.D: It overrepresents people who never exercise.

math-data-10.explanation: Gym-goers exercise more than the average adult, so the sample overestimates exercise frequency.
math-data-10.method: Ask whether every member of the target population is equally likely to be chosen.
math-data-10.speedTip: Convenience samples at specialty locations are classic bias examples.
math-data-10.commonTrap: Assuming any large sample is automatically representative.

math-data-11.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling an even number or a number greater than 4?
math-data-11.method: Use inclusion-exclusion or list the favorable outcomes.
math-data-11.speedTip: Listing is fastest on a 6-outcome die.

math-data-12.stem: A school has 50 juniors and 40 seniors. Of these, 30 juniors and 25 seniors play a sport. If a student who plays a sport is selected at random, what is the probability the student is a senior? (Enter a fraction.)
math-data-12.explanation: Sport players: 30+25=55. Seniors among them: 25. Probability=25/55=5/11.
math-data-12.method: Condition on the sport group; simplify the fraction.

math-data-13.stem: Lists P and Q have the same mean. List P: 20, 22, 23, 25, 25. List Q: 5, 15, 23, 30, 42. Which list has the greater standard deviation?

choices.C: They are equal because the means are equal.
choices.D: Cannot be determined without the formula.

math-data-13.explanation: Both are centered similarly, but Q’s values range much more widely (5 to 42 vs 20 to 25), so Q has the greater SD.
math-data-13.method: With equal means, the more dispersed list has the larger SD.
math-data-13.speedTip: Compare ranges/clustering; no heavy calculation needed on Digital SAT.
math-data-13.commonTrap: Believing equal means force equal standard deviations.

math-data-14.stem: A poll estimates that 52% of voters support a measure, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Based only on this information, which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.A: A majority of voters definitely support the measure.
choices.B: Support could reasonably be as low as 49%, so a majority is not guaranteed.
choices.C: Exactly 52% of all voters support the measure.

math-data-14.explanation: The interval is roughly 49% to 55%. Because 49% is below 50%, the poll does not guarantee majority support.
math-data-14.method: Form estimate ± MOE and see whether the claim holds throughout the interval.
math-data-14.speedTip: Check whether 50% lies inside the interval.
math-data-14.commonTrap: Treating the point estimate 52% as exact.

math-data-15.stem: In a scatterplot, as x-values increase, the y-values tend to decrease, and the points cluster tightly about a straight line. Which description fits best?
math-data-15.explanation: Decreasing trend means negative association; tight clustering means the association is strong and roughly linear.
math-data-15.method: Sign from direction; strength from how tightly points follow a line.
math-data-15.speedTip: Downward slope → negative; tight band → strong.

math-data-16.stem: What is the median of the data set 2, 5, 5, 7, 11?
math-data-16.explanation: Already ordered; with 5 values the median is the 3rd entry, which is 5.
math-data-16.method: Sort (if needed) and take the middle value for an odd count.
math-data-16.commonTrap: Averaging 5 and 7 as if the count were even.

math-data-17.stem: Event A: a student takes Physics. Event B: a student takes Calculus. Which expression represents the probability that a student takes Calculus given that the student takes Physics?
math-data-17.method: Translate “given” into the conditional bar notation with the condition after the bar.
math-data-17.speedTip: Given X → X is after the bar.
math-data-17.commonTrap: Swapping to P(A|B) or using the joint P(A and B).

math-data-18.stem: Which data set has two modes?
math-data-18.explanation: In C, both 1 and 4 appear twice and more than 9, so the set is bimodal. A has one mode; B has no mode; D has one mode.
math-data-18.method: Identify the value(s) with the highest frequency.
math-data-18.speedTip: Two distinct values tied for most frequent → two modes.
math-data-18.commonTrap: Calling a set with all unique values bimodal.

math-data-19.stem: A fair spinner is divided into 8 equal sections numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability that the spinner lands on a prime number? (Enter a fraction.)
math-data-19.explanation: Primes among 1–8: 2,3,5,7 (four numbers). P=4/8=1/2. Note: 1 is not prime.
math-data-19.method: Count favorable equally likely outcomes over 8.

math-data-20.stem: A residual for a data point on a scatterplot with a line of best fit is positive. Which statement must be true?

choices.A: The actual y-value is greater than the predicted y-value.
choices.B: The actual y-value is less than the predicted y-value.
choices.C: The slope of the line of best fit is positive.
choices.D: The point lies on the line of best fit.

math-data-20.explanation: Residual=y−ŷ. Positive means actual y exceeds the prediction, so the point is above the line.
math-data-20.speedTip: Positive residual → point above the LOBF.
math-data-20.commonTrap: Linking residual sign to the slope’s sign.

math-desmos-01.stem: The graphs of $2x+y=10$ and $x-y=2$ intersect at the point $(a,b)$. What is the value of $a+b$?
math-desmos-01.explanation: Add the equations: $3x=12$ so $x=4$. Then $4-y=2$ gives $y=2$. Intersection $(4,2)$; $a+b=6$.
math-desmos-01.speedTip: In Desmos enter $2x+y=10$ and $x-y=2$. Click the intersection; add the displayed coordinates.
math-desmos-01.commonTrap: Reading only one coordinate or subtracting instead of adding.

math-desmos-02.stem: The graph of $y=x^2-6x+8$ intersects the $x$-axis at points $(p,0)$ and $(q,0)$ with $p<q$. What is $q-p$?
math-desmos-02.speedTip: Graph $y=x^2-6x+8$; click both $x$-intercepts; subtract the smaller from the larger.
math-desmos-02.commonTrap: Reporting the larger root $4$ or the sum of roots $6$ instead of the difference.

math-desmos-03.stem: How many points of intersection does the circle $x^2+y^2=25$ have with the line $y=3x+1$?
math-desmos-03.explanation: Substitute: $x^2+(3x+1)^2=25$ gives $10x^2+6x-24=0$, or $5x^2+3x-12=0$. Discriminant $9+240=249>0$, so two real intersections.
math-desmos-03.speedTip: Graph $x^2+y^2=25$ and $y=3x+1$ together; count the intersection dots Desmos shows.
math-desmos-03.commonTrap: Assuming any line near the circle must intersect twice without verifying.

math-desmos-04.stem: The graphs of $y=x^2-4x+1$ and $y=x-3$ intersect at two points. What is the greater of the two $x$-coordinates of those intersection points?
math-desmos-04.speedTip: Graph both $y=x^2-4x+1$ and $y=x-3$; click each intersection; take the larger $x$.
math-desmos-04.commonTrap: Reporting the $y$-coordinate at that point or the smaller root $1$.

math-desmos-05.stem: Which of the following points lies in the solution region of the system $y\ge 2x-1$ and $y\le -x+5$?
math-desmos-05.explanation: For $(1,2)$: $2\ge 2(1)-1=1$ true; $2\le -1+5=4$ true. (A) $0\ge 7$ false. (B) $6\le 5$ false. (D) $4\ge 5$ false.
math-desmos-05.speedTip: In Desmos enter $y\ge 2x-1$ and $y\le -x+5$; plot each choice as a point and see which sits in the overlap.
math-desmos-05.commonTrap: Testing only one inequality and picking a boundary-looking distractor.

math-desmos-06.stem: The graphs of $y=x^2$ and $y=-x^2+8$ intersect at points with $x$-coordinates $a$ and $-a$ for some $a>0$. What is $a$?
math-desmos-06.speedTip: Graph $y=x^2$ and $y=-x^2+8$; click an intersection; read the positive $x$.

math-desmos-07.stem: A linear model $y=mx+b$ is fit to the points $(1,5)$, $(2,8)$, $(3,11)$, and $(4,14)$. What is the value of $m$ in this exact fit?
math-desmos-07.explanation: Equal steps: $\Delta y=3$ when $\Delta x=1$, so slope $m=3$. Exact line $y=3x+2$.
math-desmos-07.speedTip: Make a table in Desmos with $x_1$ and $y_1$; enter the four points. Type $y_1\sim mx_1+b$; read $m$.
math-desmos-07.commonTrap: Using an incorrect rise/run between non-adjacent points or averaging slopes wrong.

math-desmos-08.stem: How many solutions does the equation $|x-2|=|2x+1|$ have?
math-desmos-08.explanation: $|A|=|B|$ means $A=B$ or $A=-B$. Solutions $x=-3$ and $x=1/3$; both check in the original equation.
math-desmos-08.commonTrap: Forgetting a case when solving piecewise by hand.

math-desmos-09.stem: The equation $2^x=x+4$ has how many real solutions?
math-desmos-09.explanation: Graph $y=2^x$ and $y=x+4$. They meet once for a negative $x$ and once for a positive $x$ (between $2$ and $4$), so two real solutions.
math-desmos-09.speedTip: Graph $y=2^x$ and $y=x+4$; zoom out left and right; count intersection points.
math-desmos-09.commonTrap: Seeing only the obvious positive intersection and missing the negative one.

math-desmos-10.stem: The circle $(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=16$ and the line $y=1$ intersect at how many points?
math-desmos-10.explanation: Center $(1,-2)$, radius $4$. Distance from center to $y=1$ is $|1-(-2)|=3<4$, so the line cuts the circle twice.
math-desmos-10.speedTip: Graph $(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=16$ and $y=1$ in Desmos; count the intersection dots.
math-desmos-10.commonTrap: Thinking distance $3$ with radius $4$ means no intersection.

math-desmos-11.stem: If $(x,y)$ is the solution to the system $4x+3y=18$ and $2x-y=4$, what is the value of $xy$?
math-desmos-11.explanation: From the second equation, $y=2x-4$. Substitute: $4x+3(2x-4)=18$ so $10x=30$, $x=3$, $y=2$. Product $6$.
math-desmos-11.speedTip: Enter both equations in Desmos; click intersection; multiply the two coordinates.

math-desmos-12.stem: What is the minimum value of the function $f(x)=2x^2-8x+9$?
math-desmos-12.speedTip: Graph $y=2x^2-8x+9$; click the vertex; read the $y$-coordinate (minimum).
math-desmos-12.commonTrap: Reporting the vertex $x$-coordinate $2$ instead of the min value $1$.

math-desmos-13.stem: For how many integer values of $x$ is $x^2-5x+4\le 0$?
math-desmos-13.speedTip: Graph $y=x^2-5x+4$; see where it is $\le 0$ (between roots). Or table integer $x$ and count nonpositive $y$.
math-desmos-13.commonTrap: Excluding the roots (where equal to zero) and answering $2$.

math-desmos-14.stem: The line $y=3x-2$ intersects the parabola $y=x^2$ at two points. What is the sum of the $y$-coordinates of those two points?
math-desmos-14.speedTip: Graph $y=x^2$ and $y=3x-2$; click both intersections; add the $y$-values.

math-desmos-15.stem: A linear model $y=2.5x+1$ is used for data with $x$-values $2,4,6$. The corresponding observed $y$-values are $6,12,15$. For $x=6$, what is the residual (observed minus predicted)?
math-desmos-15.speedTip: In Desmos, compute $2.5\cdot 6+1$, then subtract from $15$. Or plot the line and the point $(6,15)$.
math-desmos-15.commonTrap: Reversing residual as predicted minus observed and choosing $+1$.

math-geo-01.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the acute corresponding angles measures 65°. What is the measure of the other corresponding angle?
math-geo-01.explanation: Corresponding angles formed by a transversal with parallel lines are congruent, so both measure 65°.
math-geo-01.method: Recall: corresponding (and alternate interior) angles are equal when lines are parallel.
math-geo-01.speedTip: Corresponding → same measure; consecutive interior → supplementary.
math-geo-01.commonTrap: Using the supplementary co-interior angle 115° by mistake.

math-geo-02.stem: The angles of a triangle measure 2x°, 3x°, and 4x°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the largest angle?
math-geo-02.method: Sum to 180, solve for x, evaluate the largest expression.
math-geo-02.commonTrap: Forgetting they sum to 180 and treating x as already in degrees.

math-geo-03.stem: Two similar triangles have corresponding side lengths in the ratio 3:5. The smaller triangle has a side of length 6. What is the length of the corresponding side of the larger triangle?
math-geo-03.method: Set up a proportion with corresponding sides and solve.

math-geo-04.stem: In a 30°-60°-90° triangle, the side opposite 30° has length 5. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
math-geo-04.explanation: In a 30-60-90 triangle, sides are x : x√3 : 2x. Opposite 30° is x=5, so hypotenuse=2x=10.

math-geo-05.stem: An isosceles right triangle has legs of length 7. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
math-geo-05.method: Apply the 45-45-90 ratio a : a : a√2.
math-geo-05.commonTrap: Doubling the leg (using 30-60-90’s 2x) instead of multiplying by √2.

math-geo-06.stem: A circle has radius 6. What is its circumference?

math-geo-07.stem: A circle has radius 9. What is the length of a minor arc with central angle 60°?
math-geo-07.method: Take the fraction of the circumference given by the central angle.

math-geo-08.stem: A sector of a circle with radius 4 has a central angle of 90°. What is the area of the sector?
math-geo-08.method: Take the angle fraction of the full circle’s area.
math-geo-08.commonTrap: Computing arc length (1/4)·8π=2π instead of area.

math-geo-09.stem: A cylinder has radius 3 and height 10. What is its volume?

math-geo-10.stem: A cone has radius 6 and height 8. What is its volume?

math-geo-11.stem: A sphere has radius 3. What is its volume?

math-geo-12.stem: What is the distance between the points (1,2) and (4,6) in the xy-plane?

math-geo-13.stem: What is the midpoint of the segment joining (1,2) and (7,10)?
math-geo-13.method: Average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates.
math-geo-13.speedTip: Desmos: midpoint is the average of the endpoints.

math-geo-14.stem: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle θ has length 5 and the hypotenuse has length 13. What is sin θ? (Enter a fraction.)
math-geo-14.speedTip: Desmos: asin(5/13) is optional; the ratio itself is the answer.

math-geo-15.stem: In triangle ABC, an exterior angle at C measures 110°. If one of the remote interior angles measures 40°, what is the measure of the other remote interior angle?
math-geo-15.explanation: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: 110=40+x → x=70.
math-geo-15.method: Exterior angle = sum of remote interiors.
math-geo-15.commonTrap: Thinking the exterior equals a remote interior (answering 40°) or using 180−110.

math-geo-16.stem: In right triangle DEF with right angle at E, DE=8 and DF=17. What is cos(angle at D)?
math-geo-16.explanation: Adjacent to angle D is DE=8; hypotenuse is DF=17. cos D=8/17.
math-geo-16.speedTip: Desmos: check that √(17^2−8^2)=15 for the other leg if needed.
math-geo-16.commonTrap: Using opposite/hyp=15/17 (that would be sin D).

math-geo-17.stem: A circle has diameter 10. What is its area?
math-geo-17.method: Halve the diameter, then use A=πr^2.
math-geo-17.commonTrap: Using diameter in πd^2 or giving circumference 10π.

math-geo-18.stem: A rectangular prism has dimensions 4, 5, and 6. What is its volume?
math-geo-18.commonTrap: Adding edges or computing surface area 2(20+24+30)=148.

math-geo-19.stem: Which equation represents a circle centered at the origin with radius 5?
math-geo-19.explanation: Standard form x^2+y^2=r^2 with r=5 gives x^2+y^2=25.
math-geo-19.method: Remember r^2 appears on the right-hand side.
math-geo-19.speedTip: Desmos: graph x^2+y^2=25 to see radius 5.
math-geo-19.commonTrap: Writing =5 instead of =25, or shifting the center.

math-geo-20.stem: A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and the same height. The volume of the cone is what fraction of the volume of the cylinder?
math-geo-20.explanation: V_cone=(1/3)πr^2h and V_cyl=πr^2h, so the cone is one-third of the cylinder.
math-geo-20.method: Compare the formulas directly when r and h match.
math-geo-20.speedTip: Remember: three cones fill one cylinder with the same base and height.
math-geo-20.commonTrap: Confusing with sphere/cylinder relations or answering 1/2.

math-linear-01.stem: If 3(2x − 5) + 4 = 5x − 7, what is the value of x?
math-linear-01.explanation: Distribute: 6x − 15 + 4 = 5x − 7 → 6x − 11 = 5x − 7. Subtract 5x from both sides: x − 11 = −7. Add 11: x = 4.
math-linear-01.speedTip: Distribute carefully, then isolate x in two moves.
math-linear-01.commonTrap: Forgetting to multiply 3 by −5 yields 6x − 5 + 4 = 5x − 7 → x = −6, which is not listed; students who then flip a sign may pick 8.

math-linear-02.stem: Solve for n: (2n − 3)/5 = (n + 7)/3. Enter the value of n.
math-linear-02.speedTip: Cross-multiply to clear both denominators at once.
math-linear-02.commonTrap: Writing 5(2n−3)=3(n+7) by flipping the multipliers, getting n = −36/7.

math-linear-03.stem: A rideshare charges a $3.50 base fee plus $0.80 per mile. Maya's trip costs $15.50. How many miles did she travel?
math-linear-03.speedTip: Isolate the per-mile term: (total − base) ÷ rate.
math-linear-03.commonTrap: Dividing 15.50 by 0.80 without subtracting the base fee, getting about 19 (choice D).

math-linear-04.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to −4(x − 2) ≥ 12?
math-linear-04.explanation: −4(x − 2) ≥ 12 → −4x + 8 ≥ 12 → −4x ≥ 4. Divide by −4 and reverse the inequality: x ≤ −1.
math-linear-04.speedTip: Remember to flip the inequality when dividing by a negative.
math-linear-04.commonTrap: Forgetting to reverse the inequality and choosing x ≥ −1 (choice B).

math-linear-05.stem: If 5 − 2k < 3k + 20 and k is an integer, what is the least possible value of k?
math-linear-05.speedTip: Solve the inequality, then pick the smallest integer strictly greater than the bound.
math-linear-05.commonTrap: Using k ≥ −3 and entering −3, which does not satisfy the strict inequality.

math-linear-06.stem: A line passes through the points (−2, 5) and (4, −1). What is the slope of the line?
math-linear-06.speedTip: m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1); keep the order of points consistent.
math-linear-06.commonTrap: Swapping numerator and denominator or reversing only one difference, getting −1/2 or 1.

math-linear-07.stem: The graph of y = −(3/4)x + 6 intersects the x-axis at point P. What is the x-coordinate of P?
math-linear-07.speedTip: X-intercept means y = 0; solve quickly or use Desmos to graph and read the intercept.
math-linear-07.commonTrap: Reporting the y-intercept 6 instead of the x-intercept 8 (choice C).

math-linear-08.stem: What is the slope of the line 5x − 2y = 14?
math-linear-08.explanation: Solve for y: −2y = −5x + 14 → y = (5/2)x − 7. Slope is 5/2.
math-linear-08.speedTip: Convert Ax + By = C to slope-intercept: m = −A/B. Here m = −5/(−2) = 5/2.
math-linear-08.commonTrap: Using A/B = 5/2 with wrong sign, or reporting −5/2.

math-linear-09.stem: Which of the following lines is parallel to the line y = −2x + 9?
math-linear-09.explanation: Parallel lines share the same slope. The given line has slope −2. Choice B also has slope −2. Choice D: 4y = −2x + 8 → y = −(1/2)x + 2, slope −1/2. Choice A has slope 1/2 (perpendicular). Choice C has slope 2.
math-linear-09.speedTip: Match slopes only; intercepts can differ.
math-linear-09.commonTrap: Picking the perpendicular slope 1/2 (choice A) or same intercept (choice C).

math-linear-10.stem: Line ℓ passes through (0, −4) and is perpendicular to the line 3x + 6y = 12. Which equation represents line ℓ?
math-linear-10.explanation: Rewrite 3x + 6y = 12 → 6y = −3x + 12 → y = −(1/2)x + 2. Slope of given line is −1/2, so perpendicular slope is 2. Through (0, −4): y = 2x − 4.
math-linear-10.speedTip: Perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal; y-intercept is given by the point (0, −4).
math-linear-10.commonTrap: Using the same slope −1/2 (choice B) instead of the negative reciprocal.

math-linear-11.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = −3x + 11. What is the value of f(−2)?
math-linear-11.speedTip: Substitute carefully with parentheses around negative inputs.

math-linear-12.stem: For the linear function g(x) = 4x − 9, what is the value of x for which g(x) = 15?
math-linear-12.speedTip: Set the expression equal to 15 and solve; or use Desmos table/slider.
math-linear-12.commonTrap: Solving 4x − 9 = −15 or dividing incorrectly to get 24/4 with leftover −9.

math-linear-13.stem: The linear model C = 2.5h + 40 estimates the cost C, in dollars, of renting a canoe for h hours. According to the model, what does the number 2.5 represent?

choices.A: The canoe rental costs $2.50 for each hour after a $40 base fee.
choices.B: The canoe can be rented for at most 2.5 hours.
choices.C: The total cost decreases by $2.50 each hour.

math-linear-13.explanation: In C = mh + b, m = 2.5 is the rate of change (cost per hour) and b = 40 is the fixed base fee. So each additional hour adds $2.50.
math-linear-13.speedTip: Slope = rate per unit of the input; intercept = starting value when input is 0.
math-linear-13.commonTrap: Confusing slope with the intercept (thinking 2.5 is a base fee).

math-linear-14.stem: The table shows values of a linear function h. When x = 1, h(x) = 7; when x = 2, h(x) = 4; when x = 3, h(x) = 1. Which equation defines h?
math-linear-14.speedTip: Find slope from any two rows, then back-solve for b with one point.
math-linear-14.commonTrap: Using y-intercept as the first table value 7 without adjusting (choice B).

math-linear-15.stem: In the xy-plane, the graph of the linear function f intersects the y-axis at (0, −3) and has slope 4/5. Which of the following is an equation of f?
math-linear-15.explanation: Slope-intercept form: f(x) = mx + b with m = 4/5 and b = −3 → f(x) = (4/5)x − 3.
math-linear-15.speedTip: Y-intercept is b; do not flip slope fraction.
math-linear-15.commonTrap: Writing +3 instead of −3 (choice D) or reciprocating the slope (choice B).

math-linear-16.stem: Seven less than three times a number is equal to the number increased by 17. What is the number?
math-linear-16.speedTip: Translate phrase-by-phrase: "seven less than three times" → 3x − 7.
math-linear-16.commonTrap: Writing 7 − 3x instead of 3x − 7, which yields a negative answer.

math-linear-17.stem: If (1/2)(6x − 4) − (1/3)(3x + 9) = 5, what is the value of x?
math-linear-17.speedTip: Clear each parentheses product separately before combining.
math-linear-17.commonTrap: Distributing the minus sign incorrectly across (x+3).

math-linear-18.stem: A printer can print at most 40 pages per minute. Let p be the number of pages printed in t minutes at a constant rate of 40 pages per minute. Which inequality represents all possible values of p for a job that must finish in no more than 6 minutes?
math-linear-18.explanation: Maximum pages in 6 minutes: 40 · 6 = 240. So p ≤ 240.
math-linear-18.speedTip: "At most" and "no more than" both translate to ≤.
math-linear-18.commonTrap: Using ≥ because the rate is "at most 40," confusing rate with total pages.

math-linear-19.stem: A line passes through (2, 11) and (5, 5). What is the y-intercept of the line?
math-linear-19.speedTip: Slope first, then point-slope; or Desmos: enter the two points and read b.
math-linear-19.commonTrap: Reporting the slope −2 instead of the intercept, or using x-intercept.

math-linear-20.stem: What is the equation of the line that passes through (−3, 7) and is parallel to 2x − y = 10?
math-linear-20.explanation: 2x − y = 10 → y = 2x − 10, slope 2. Parallel: slope 2 through (−3, 7): 7 = 2(−3) + b → 7 = −6 + b → b = 13. So y = 2x + 13.
math-linear-20.speedTip: Rewrite given line to get slope, then plug the point into y = mx + b.
math-linear-20.commonTrap: Using slope −1/2 (negative reciprocal, which is perpendicular) — choice C.

math-linear-21.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x − 5. If f(a) = 9 and f(b) = −1, what is the value of a − b?
math-linear-21.speedTip: Solve each equation separately, then subtract; or note a − b = (f(a) − f(b))/2 since slope is 2.
math-linear-21.commonTrap: Computing a + b = 9 or f(a) − f(b) = 10 without dividing by the slope (choice D).

math-linear-22.stem: For what value of c is the solution set of 3x − c ≤ 2x + 5 identical to the solution set of x ≤ 8?
math-linear-22.speedTip: Reduce the inequality to x ≤ (something) and match the bound.

math-linear-23.stem: A linear function f satisfies f(2) = 11 and f(5) = 2. Which of the following could be an expression for f(x)?
math-linear-23.speedTip: Two points determine slope and intercept uniquely for a linear function.
math-linear-23.commonTrap: Using b = f(2) = 11 without adjusting for the slope term (choice B).

math-linear-24.stem: If 4(2x + 1) = 3(x − 5) + 29, what is the value of 2x + 1?
math-linear-24.explanation: Expand: 8x + 4 = 3x − 15 + 29 → 8x + 4 = 3x + 14 → 5x = 10 → x = 2. Then 2x + 1 = 5. Alternatively, notice left side is 4(2x+1), so once you know 2x+1, but solving for x first is fine.
math-linear-24.speedTip: Question asks for 2x+1, not x — compute x then substitute, or divide both sides strategically.
math-linear-24.commonTrap: Stopping at x = 2 and selecting 2 (choice A) instead of evaluating 2x + 1.

math-linear-25.stem: A tank contains 48 gallons of water. Water is drained at a constant rate of 1.5 gallons per minute. After how many minutes will the tank contain 12 gallons?
math-linear-25.commonTrap: Dividing 12 by 1.5 to get 8, or 48/1.5 = 32 (time to empty completely).

math-nonlinear-01.stem: A bacterial culture starts with 240 cells and triples every 4 hours. Which expression gives the number of cells after t hours?
math-nonlinear-01.explanation: The culture triples once every 4 hours, so after t hours there are t/4 growth intervals. The amount is 240(3)^{t/4}.
math-nonlinear-01.method: Use a·b^{t/p} with initial a, growth factor b, and period p.
math-nonlinear-01.speedTip: Desmos: graph y=240*3^(x/4) and verify (4,720) and (8,2160).
math-nonlinear-01.commonTrap: Writing 3^{4t} or treating the change as linear addition.

math-nonlinear-02.explanation: Square both sides: 3x+1=(x−1)^2 → 0=x^2−5x → x(x−5)=0, so x=0 or x=5. The domain requires x−1≥0, hence x≥1. Only x=5 works: √16=4=5−1.
math-nonlinear-02.method: Square, solve the polynomial, then reject roots that violate the domain or fail substitution.
math-nonlinear-02.speedTip: Desmos: find intersections of y=√(3x+1) and y=x−1 for x≥1.
math-nonlinear-02.commonTrap: Keeping the extraneous root x=0 created by squaring.

math-nonlinear-03.stem: Solve 2/(x−3)=5/(x+1). What is the value of x?
math-nonlinear-03.explanation: Cross-multiply: 2(x+1)=5(x−3) → 2x+2=5x−15 → 17=3x → x=17/3. The domain excludes x=3 and x=−1, so 17/3 is valid.
math-nonlinear-03.method: Clear denominators, solve the resulting equation, then check excluded values.
math-nonlinear-03.speedTip: Reject any answer that makes a denominator zero.
math-nonlinear-03.commonTrap: Accepting a root that equals an excluded value.

math-nonlinear-04.stem: If |2x−5|=7, what is the sum of all real solutions for x?
math-nonlinear-04.explanation: Cases: 2x−5=7 or 2x−5=−7 → x=6 or x=−1. Sum=5.
math-nonlinear-04.speedTip: The solutions are symmetric about x=5/2, so their sum is 5.
math-nonlinear-04.commonTrap: Solving only the positive case and reporting 6.

math-nonlinear-05.stem: The equation x^3−6x^2+5x+12=0 has a root at x=−1. What is the product of the other two roots?
math-nonlinear-05.explanation: Synthetic division by −1 on coefficients 1, −6, 5, 12 yields quotient x^2−7x+12 with remainder 0. Factoring gives (x−3)(x−4). The other roots are 3 and 4; product=12.
math-nonlinear-05.method: Use the known root to factor the cubic, then solve the quadratic factor.
math-nonlinear-05.speedTip: After synthetic division of a monic cubic, the constant of the quadratic is the product of the remaining roots.
math-nonlinear-05.commonTrap: Applying Vieta to all three roots without removing the known factor.

math-nonlinear-06.stem: Quantity y varies inversely with x. When x=4, y=15. What is y when x=10?
math-nonlinear-06.explanation: Inverse variation means xy=k. Then 4·15=60, so when x=10, y=60/10=6.
math-nonlinear-06.method: Find k=xy from the given pair, then solve for the unknown.
math-nonlinear-06.speedTip: Quick check: doubling x halves y; here x grows by 2.5, so y becomes 15/2.5=6.
math-nonlinear-06.commonTrap: Using direct variation y=kx instead of xy=k.

math-nonlinear-07.stem: If 5^{2x}=125^{x−1}, what is the value of x?
math-nonlinear-07.method: Express both sides with the same base, then set exponents equal.
math-nonlinear-07.speedTip: Desmos: graph y=5^(2x) and y=125^(x−1); read the intersection x-value.
math-nonlinear-07.commonTrap: Equating 2x with x−1 without rewriting the base 125.

math-nonlinear-08.stem: What is the solution to √(x+12)=x? (Enter the real solution.)
math-nonlinear-08.explanation: Square: x+12=x^2 → x^2−x−12=0 → (x−4)(x+3)=0. Candidates 4 and −3. Domain of √ requires x≥0 (and original right side x≥0), so only x=4. Check: √16=4.
math-nonlinear-08.method: Square carefully, then discard roots outside the radical domain.
math-nonlinear-08.speedTip: Desmos intersection of y=√(x+12) and y=x immediately shows x=4.

math-nonlinear-09.stem: Solve 1/(x−4)+1/(x+4)=1/3. What is the sum of the solutions?
math-nonlinear-09.explanation: Common denominator: (x+4+x−4)/(x^2−16)=1/3 → 2x/(x^2−16)=1/3 → 6x=x^2−16 → x^2−6x−16=0 → (x−8)(x+2)=0. Solutions 8 and −2 (neither ±4). Sum=6.
math-nonlinear-09.method: Combine fractions, clear the remaining denominator, solve, and check excluded values.
math-nonlinear-09.speedTip: Desmos: graph both sides (or the cleared equation) and sum the valid intersection x-values.
math-nonlinear-09.commonTrap: Including x=±4 even though they make a denominator zero.

math-nonlinear-10.explanation: Require 2x−1≥0 so x≥1/2. Case x+3=2x−1 → x=4 (valid: |7|=7). Case x+3=−(2x−1) → 3x=−2 → x=−2/3, which fails x≥1/2. Only x=4.
math-nonlinear-10.method: First impose that the right-hand side is nonnegative, then solve the two cases.
math-nonlinear-10.speedTip: Plug choices into both sides; only D matches.
math-nonlinear-10.commonTrap: Accepting a case solution that makes 2x−1 negative.

math-nonlinear-11.stem: If y varies inversely as x and y=8 when x=3, what is y when x=12?
math-nonlinear-11.method: Compute k from the given pair, then evaluate y=k/x.
math-nonlinear-11.speedTip: x is multiplied by 4, so y is divided by 4: 8/4=2.
math-nonlinear-11.commonTrap: Multiplying instead of dividing when x increases.

math-nonlinear-12.stem: A function gives the table of values: x=1,2,3,4 and y=5,11,21,35. Which equation could define the function?
math-nonlinear-12.explanation: Substitute each x into the choices. For B: 2(1)^2+3=5, 2(2)^2+3=11, 2(3)^2+3=21, 2(4)^2+3=35, matching the table. A gives 17 at x=3, not 21. C gives 29 at x=3, not 21. D gives 12 at x=2, not 11. Only B fits all values.
math-nonlinear-12.method: Plug each x into the answer choices until only one matches the entire table.
math-nonlinear-12.speedTip: First differences 6,10,14 and second differences 4,4 suggest a quadratic—scan for a quadratic choice.
math-nonlinear-12.commonTrap: Matching only the first row and ignoring later values.

math-nonlinear-13.stem: The function A(t)=500(0.85)^t models the amount of a substance remaining after t years. Which statement is true?

choices.A: The substance increases by 85% each year.
choices.B: The substance decreases by 15% each year.
choices.C: The substance decreases by 85% each year.
choices.D: The substance increases by 15% each year.

math-nonlinear-13.explanation: The factor 0.85 means each year the amount is 85% of the previous year, so it loses 15% per year.
math-nonlinear-13.method: Interpret b in a·b^t: if 0<b<1, percent decrease is (1−b)·100%.
math-nonlinear-13.commonTrap: Confusing the remaining 85% with an 85% decrease.

math-nonlinear-14.stem: If ∛(2x−1)=3, what is the value of x?
math-nonlinear-14.method: Undo the cube root by cubing, then solve the linear equation.
math-nonlinear-14.speedTip: Desmos: intersection of y=∛(2x−1) and y=3.

math-nonlinear-15.stem: If 4^x=8^{x−1}, what is the value of x?
math-nonlinear-15.speedTip: Desmos: graph y=4^x and y=8^(x−1); read x at the intersection.
math-nonlinear-15.commonTrap: Setting x equal to x−1 without converting bases.

math-nonlinear-16.stem: Solve x/(x+1)=2−1/(x+1). How many real solutions does the equation have?
math-nonlinear-16.explanation: Multiply through by x+1 (x≠−1): x=2(x+1)−1 → x=2x+2−1 → 0=x+1 → x=−1. But x=−1 is excluded, so there is no solution.
math-nonlinear-16.method: Clear the denominator, solve, and test against excluded values; an only-candidate that is excluded means zero solutions.
math-nonlinear-16.speedTip: If algebra returns exactly an excluded value, conclude no solution immediately.
math-nonlinear-16.commonTrap: Reporting the extraneous value x=−1 as a solution.

math-nonlinear-17.explanation: Points equidistant from −3 and 5 lie at the midpoint: (−3+5)/2=1. Check: |1+3|=4 and |1−5|=4.
math-nonlinear-17.method: For |x−a|=|x−b|, the solution is the midpoint of a and b (here a=−3, b=5).
math-nonlinear-17.commonTrap: Choosing one of the endpoints −3 or 5 instead of the midpoint.

math-nonlinear-18.stem: For f(x)=x^3−2x^2−x+2, it is given that f(2)=0. If f(x)=(x−2)(x^2+ax+b), what is the value of a+b?
math-nonlinear-18.explanation: Synthetic division by 2 on 1, −2, −1, 2: bring 1; add 2 → 0; add 0 → −1; add −2 → 0. Quotient x^2+0x−1, so a=0, b=−1, and a+b=−1.
math-nonlinear-18.method: Divide the cubic by (x−2) to read a and b from the quadratic factor.
math-nonlinear-18.speedTip: Synthetic division with root 2 is the fastest path to a and b.
math-nonlinear-18.commonTrap: Sign errors in synthetic division producing a=0, b=1.

math-nonlinear-19.stem: For a positive constant k, the graph of y=k/x in the xy-plane lies in which quadrants?
math-nonlinear-19.explanation: If k>0, x and y must have the same sign: both positive (QI) or both negative (QIII).
math-nonlinear-19.method: Sign analysis of y=k/x when k>0.
math-nonlinear-19.speedTip: Desmos: graph y=1/x and note the branches in QI and QIII.
math-nonlinear-19.commonTrap: Confusing with y=−k/x, which occupies QII and QIV.

math-nonlinear-20.stem: If 3^{x+2}=81, what is the value of x?
math-nonlinear-20.method: Rewrite 81 as a power of 3, then equate exponents.
math-nonlinear-20.speedTip: Desmos: intersection of y=3^(x+2) and y=81.
math-nonlinear-20.commonTrap: Solving 3x+2=81 as if the equation were linear.

math-systems-01.stem:
What is the solution (x, y) to the system below?
2x + y = 11
x − y = 1
math-systems-01.explanation: Add the equations: 3x = 12 → x = 4. Then 4 − y = 1 → y = 3. Solution (4, 3).
math-systems-01.speedTip: Adding cancels y immediately here; Desmos graph both lines and read the intersection.
math-systems-01.commonTrap: Subtracting instead of adding and getting x = 5 or switching coordinates.

math-systems-02.stem: If 3x − 2y = 4 and x + 2y = 12, what is the value of x?
math-systems-02.explanation: Add: 4x = 16 → x = 4. (Then y = 4 from second equation.)
math-systems-02.speedTip: Opposite y-coefficients: add to eliminate y in one step.
math-systems-02.commonTrap: Adding incorrectly to get x = 8, or finding y = 4 and selecting that.

math-systems-03.stem:
The system
y = 2x − 5
4x − 2y = 10
has how many solutions?
math-systems-03.explanation: Substitute y = 2x − 5 into second: 4x − 2(2x − 5) = 10 → 4x − 4x + 10 = 10 → 10 = 10, always true. The second equation is equivalent to the first (divide by 2: 2x − y = 5 → y = 2x − 5). Infinitely many solutions.
math-systems-03.speedTip: If one equation is a multiple of the other, infinite solutions; Desmos shows coincident lines.
math-systems-03.commonTrap: Seeing identical slopes and wrongly saying no solution (parallel distinct lines).

math-systems-04.stem: Which of the following systems has no solution?
math-systems-04.explanation: Same slope 3, different intercepts → parallel distinct lines → no solution. B is the same line (infinite). C intersects (perp-ish). D has unique solution.
math-systems-04.speedTip: No solution ⟺ same slope, different y-intercept. Desmos makes this obvious.
math-systems-04.commonTrap: Picking B, which actually has infinitely many solutions.

math-systems-05.stem: If 5x + 3y = −13 and 2x − y = 8, what is the value of y?
math-systems-05.explanation: From 2x − y = 8, y = 2x − 8. Substitute into first: 5x + 3(2x − 8) = −13 → 5x + 6x − 24 = −13 → 11x = 11 → x = 1. Then y = 2(1) − 8 = −6. Elimination: multiply second by 3 → 6x − 3y = 24; add to first: 11x = 11 → x = 1; y = −6.
math-systems-05.speedTip: Isolate y from the second equation (coefficient −1) then substitute.

math-systems-06.stem: A school club sold adult tickets for $8 and student tickets for $5. They sold 120 tickets and collected $765. How many adult tickets were sold?
math-systems-06.explanation: Let a = adult, s = student. a + s = 120, 8a + 5s = 765. From first, s = 120 − a. Then 8a + 5(120 − a) = 765 → 8a + 600 − 5a = 765 → 3a = 165 → a = 55.
math-systems-06.speedTip: Word systems: define variables clearly; elimination also works after multiplying the ticket-count equation by 5.
math-systems-06.commonTrap: Solving for student tickets (65) and picking that (choice C).

math-systems-07.stem: Two lines in the xy-plane are graphed. One has equation y = −x + 6 and the other has equation y = 2x − 3. What is the y-coordinate of their point of intersection?
math-systems-07.speedTip: Graph both in Desmos and read the intersection; or set expressions equal.
math-systems-07.commonTrap: Reporting the x-coordinate (also 3 here—verify both); or picking an intercept like 6.

math-systems-08.stem:
For the system
x + 4y = 10
3x − 2y = −12
what is the value of x + y?
math-systems-08.speedTip: After finding x and y, don't forget the question asks for x + y.
math-systems-08.commonTrap: Choosing x = −2 or y = 3 if those appeared; here students may stop and pick 0 by arithmetic slip.

math-systems-09.stem: The graphs of 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x + 6y = k in the xy-plane intersect at infinitely many points when k equals which value?
math-systems-09.explanation: The second equation must be a scalar multiple of the first. Multiplying the first by 2 gives 4x + 6y = 24, so k = 24.
math-systems-09.speedTip: For infinite solutions, constants must scale by the same factor as the coefficients.
math-systems-09.commonTrap: Using k = 12 (same constant) which actually makes inconsistent or not multiple—wait, 4x+6y=12 is parallel distinct → no solution.

math-systems-10.stem: A chemist mixes a 20% acid solution with a 50% acid solution to make 30 liters of a 40% acid solution. How many liters of the 50% solution are used?
math-systems-10.explanation: Let a = liters of 20%, b = liters of 50%. a + b = 30, 0.20a + 0.50b = 0.40(30) = 12. Multiply second by 10: 2a + 5b = 120. From first a = 30 − b: 2(30 − b) + 5b = 120 → 60 − 2b + 5b = 120 → 3b = 60 → b = 20.
math-systems-10.speedTip: Clear decimals by multiplying the percent equation by 10 or 100.
math-systems-10.commonTrap: Finding the 20% amount (10 L) and selecting that (choice A).

math-systems-11.stem:
If the system
y = mx + 4
2x + y = 10
has no solution, what is the value of m?
math-systems-11.explanation: Rewrite second as y = −2x + 10. For no solution, slopes equal but intercepts differ: m = −2 (and 4 ≠ 10, which is true).
math-systems-11.speedTip: No solution when slopes match and intercepts differ; Desmos: second line has slope −2.
math-systems-11.commonTrap: Choosing m = 2 or the intercept value 4.

math-systems-12.stem:
What is the y-coordinate of the solution to the system
y = 5x − 8
y = −x + 4?
math-systems-12.speedTip: Graph y=5x−8 and y=−x+4 in Desmos; read the intersection y-value.
math-systems-12.commonTrap: Reporting x = 2 (not listed) or the intercept 4 (choice D).

math-systems-13.stem: A theater sold 200 tickets for a play. Adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $7. The total revenue was $2,090. How many child tickets were sold?
math-systems-13.speedTip: After setting up, eliminate the adult variable; check 12(138)+7(62)=1656+434=2090.
math-systems-13.commonTrap: Finding adult tickets 138 and entering that.

math-systems-14.stem: Which ordered pair (x, y) satisfies both 3x − y = 9 and x + 2y = 10?
math-systems-14.explanation: From first, y = 3x − 9. Plug into second: x + 2(3x − 9) = 10 → x + 6x − 18 = 10 → 7x = 28 → x = 4. y = 12 − 9 = 3. Check choice B in both equations.
math-systems-14.speedTip: On MC, plug each ordered pair into both equations — often faster than solving.
math-systems-14.commonTrap: Picking (2,4) which satisfies x+2y=10 but not 3x−y=9 (3(2)−4=2≠9).

math-systems-15.stem:
For which value of k does the system
y = kx + 3
y = 4x − 1
have no solution?
math-systems-15.explanation: No solution when slopes are equal and intercepts differ: k = 4 (and 3 ≠ −1).
math-systems-15.speedTip: Same slope, different intercept → parallel → no intersection.
math-systems-15.commonTrap: Choosing k = 3 because that matches an intercept constant.

math-systems-16.stem: If 4x + 5y = 23 and 2x − y = 1, what is the value of 6x + 4y?
math-systems-16.explanation: Notice 6x + 4y = (4x + 5y) + (2x − y) = 23 + 1 = 24. No need to solve for x and y individually.
math-systems-16.speedTip: Look for linear combinations of the given equations that match the expression asked.
math-systems-16.commonTrap: Solving the full system (x=2, y=3) and then mis-adding 6(2)+4(3).

math-systems-17.stem: Line p has equation 3x + y = 7. Line q is perpendicular to line p and passes through (1, −2). Which of the following is an equation of line q?
math-systems-17.explanation: Line p: y = −3x + 7, slope −3. Perpendicular slope = 1/3. Through (1, −2): −2 = (1/3)(1) + b → b = −2 − 1/3 = −7/3. So y = (1/3)x − 7/3.
math-systems-17.speedTip: This blends systems setup with perpendicular slopes; Desmos can verify the intersection angle visually.
math-systems-17.commonTrap: Using slope −3 again (choice A) or slope 3 (choice C).

math-systems-18.stem: A store sells notebooks for $4 each and pens for $2 each. Elena buys a total of 15 notebooks and pens and spends $42. How many notebooks did she buy?
math-systems-18.explanation: n + p = 15, 4n + 2p = 42. Divide money eq by 2: 2n + p = 21. Subtract first: (2n + p) − (n + p) = 21 − 15 → n = 6.
math-systems-18.speedTip: Divide the money equation by 2 first to simplify elimination.

math-systems-19.stem: In the xy-plane, the lines y = (1/2)x + 5 and y = −x + 14 intersect. What is the x-coordinate of the intersection point?
math-systems-19.speedTip: Desmos: graph both; tap intersection to read x. Algebra: set right-hand sides equal.
math-systems-19.commonTrap: Getting (3/2)x = 9 and forgetting to multiply by 2/3, picking 9 (not listed) or 4.

math-systems-20.stem:
The system
2x + 3y = 17
x − y = 1
is graphed in the xy-plane. What is the sum of the x- and y-coordinates of the intersection point?
math-systems-20.explanation: From x − y = 1, x = y + 1. Substitute: 2(y + 1) + 3y = 17 → 2y + 2 + 3y = 17 → 5y = 15 → y = 3. Then x = 4. Sum = 7.
math-systems-20.speedTip: Graph 2x+3y=17 and x−y=1 in Desmos; add the intersection coordinates.
math-systems-20.commonTrap: Reporting x = 4 or y = 3 instead of the sum 7.

math-m1-01.stem: If $3x+7=22$, what is the value of $x$?
math-m1-01.commonTrap: Forgetting to subtract $7$ and dividing $22$ by $3$.

math-m1-02.stem: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio $5:2$. If $15$ cups of flour are used, how many cups of sugar are needed?

math-m1-04.stem: A line passes through $(0,4)$ and $(2,10)$. Which equation represents the line?
math-m1-04.commonTrap: Using run/rise or subtracting coordinates in the wrong order.

math-m1-05.stem: What is the $y$-coordinate of the solution to the system $x+y=9$ and $x-y=1$?
math-m1-05.speedTip: Add the equations to eliminate $y$, then back-substitute.

math-m1-06.stem: A taxi charges a $\$3$ flat fee plus $\$2$ per mile. How many miles can be traveled for exactly $\$27$?
math-m1-06.commonTrap: Forgetting the flat fee and computing $27/2$.

math-m1-07.stem: A store sold $40$ red shirts and $60$ blue shirts. What percent of the shirts sold were red?
math-m1-07.speedTip: Total is $100$; red percent is immediate.

math-m1-08.stem: A rectangle has length $12$ and width $5$. What is its perimeter?

math-m1-09.stem: If $\dfrac{2}{3}x=18$, what is the value of $x$?

math-m1-10.speedTip: Add exponents when multiplying same base.
math-m1-10.commonTrap: Multiplying exponents to get $8$ or bases to get $9^6$.

math-m1-12.stem: A car travels $150$ miles in $2.5$ hours at a constant speed. What is the speed in miles per hour?

math-m1-13.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) of $4$, $8$, and $x$ is $10$. What is $x$?

math-m1-14.stem: Two complementary angles have measures $3k$ degrees and $2k$ degrees. What is the value of $k$?

math-m1-15.stem: If $y=2x$ and $3x+y=20$, what is the value of $x$?

math-m1-16.stem: A price increases from $\$50$ to $\$65$. What is the percent increase?
math-m1-16.commonTrap: Dividing by the new price $65$ or reporting the dollar change as $15\%$.

math-m1-18.stem: One solution of $x^2-5x+6=0$ is $x=2$. What is the other solution?
math-m1-18.speedTip: Find factors of $6$ that sum to $5$: $2$ and $3$.
math-m1-18.commonTrap: Using the quadratic formula incorrectly and getting a non-integer.

math-m1-19.stem: In similar triangles, corresponding sides are proportional. If one triangle has sides $3,4,5$ and a similar triangle has shortest side $9$, what is its longest side?
math-m1-19.commonTrap: Adding $6$ to each side or scaling the wrong side.

math-m1-20.stem: A line of best fit is $y=1.2x+8$, where $x$ is hours studied and $y$ is test score. According to the model, what is the predicted score increase for each additional hour studied?
math-m1-20.explanation: Slope $1.2$ is the change in $y$ per unit $x$.
math-m1-20.commonTrap: Choosing the intercept $8$ as the per-hour change.

math-m1-21.stem: A rectangular box has dimensions $4$, $3$, and $2$. What is its volume?

math-m1-22.stem: The graph of $y=(x-3)^2+2$ has its vertex at which point?

math-m2h-01.stem: The system $2x+ky=8$ and $4x+6y=16$ has infinitely many solutions. What is the value of $k$?
math-m2h-01.explanation: The second equation is $2$ times the first when $k=3$: $2(2x+3y)=4x+6y$ and $2\cdot 8=16$.
math-m2h-01.speedTip: Second equation must be a constant multiple of the first.
math-m2h-01.commonTrap: Choosing $k=6$ from matching the $y$ coefficient alone.

math-m2h-02.stem: For what positive value of $c$ does $x^2-6x+c=0$ have exactly one real solution?

math-m2h-03.stem: A jacket costs $\$80$. It is discounted by $25\%$, then a $10\%$ sales tax is applied to the discounted price. What is the final price?
math-m2h-03.speedTip: Discount first, then tax on the new price — not on original.
math-m2h-03.commonTrap: Applying a net $35\%$ off or taxing the original then discounting.

math-m2h-04.stem: A population doubles every $6$ years. If the population is $1{,}200$ now, which expression gives the population after $t$ years?
math-m2h-04.explanation: Number of doublings is $t/6$, so multiply by $2^{t/6}$.

math-m2h-05.stem: If $\dfrac{x}{x-2}=3$, what is the value of $x$?

math-m2h-07.stem: Which of the following is an equation of a circle with center $(-2,5)$ and radius $3$?
math-m2h-07.speedTip: Radius squared on the right; center signs flip inside the parentheses.
math-m2h-07.commonTrap: Leaving radius as $3$ instead of $9$, or flipping center signs wrong.

math-m2h-08.stem: In a right triangle, $\sin \theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$. If the side adjacent to $\theta$ is $12$, what is the hypotenuse?
math-m2h-08.explanation: $\sin=\text{opp}/\text{hyp}=5/13$, so hypotenuse $=13$. Consistent with a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle.
math-m2h-08.speedTip: Read hypotenuse from the sine ratio when opposite is $5$.

math-m2h-09.stem: If $(x-4)$ is a factor of $x^2+bx-12$, what is $b$?

math-m2h-10.stem: How many real solutions $(x,y)$ does the system $y=x^2$ and $y=2x+3$ have?
math-m2h-10.speedTip: Set equal; quadratic with positive discriminant means two solutions.

math-m2h-11.stem: An investment of $\$500$ increases by $20\%$ in year 1 and then decreases by $20\%$ in year 2. What is the value in dollars at the end of year 2?

math-m2h-12.stem: A data set has mean $50$ and median $42$. Which of the following is most likely true?

choices.B: The distribution is skewed right (positively skewed).
choices.C: The distribution is skewed left (negatively skewed).

math-m2h-12.explanation: Mean > median typically indicates a right skew (high outliers pull the mean up).
math-m2h-12.speedTip: Compare mean and median: mean larger means pull to the right.

math-m2h-13.stem: Two similar triangles have side lengths in the ratio $2:5$. What is the ratio of their areas?
math-m2h-13.explanation: Area ratio is the square of the side ratio: $2^2:5^2=4:25$.
math-m2h-13.commonTrap: Using the side ratio $2:5$ or cubing for volume $8:125$.

math-m2h-14.stem: What is the sum of all solutions to $|2x-4|=10$?

math-m2h-15.speedTip: Square both sides, then solve; always check.
math-m2h-15.commonTrap: Forgetting to subtract 1 before dividing by 2, or reporting 24 from 2x+1=25 without solving for x.

math-m2h-16.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $-3\le 2x+1\le 7$?
math-m2h-16.commonTrap: Forgetting to adjust all three parts.

math-m2h-17.stem: In a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, the side opposite $30^\circ$ is $5$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
math-m2h-17.explanation: In a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle, hypotenuse $=2\times$ shorter leg $=10$.
math-m2h-17.commonTrap: Multiplying by $\sqrt{3}$ (longer leg) instead of by $2$.

math-m2h-18.stem: An object's height in feet is $h(t)=-16t^2+64t+80$. At what time $t>0$ does it hit the ground ($h=0$)?
math-m2h-18.speedTip: Divide by $-16$, factor; discard the negative root.
math-m2h-18.commonTrap: Using vertex time $t=2$ as landing time.

math-m2h-19.stem: A liquid has density $1.25$ grams per milliliter. What is the mass, in grams, of $0.40$ liters of this liquid? (Note: $1$ liter $=1000$ milliliters.)
math-m2h-19.speedTip: Convert L to mL first, then multiply by density.

math-m2h-20.stem: If $x+y=10$ and $xy=21$, what is the value of $x^2+y^2$?

math-m2h-21.stem: In right triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $C$, $\cos A=\dfrac{3}{5}$. What is $\sin B$?
math-m2h-21.explanation: Angles $A$ and $B$ are complementary, so $\sin B=\cos A=3/5$.
math-m2h-21.speedTip: $\sin B=\cos A$ for complementary acute angles.
math-m2h-21.commonTrap: Computing the other-leg ratio $4/5=\sin A=\cos B$ instead.

math-m2h-22.stem: Solution A is $30\%$ acid and solution B is $60\%$ acid. How many liters of A must be mixed with $10$ liters of B to obtain a $40\%$ acid mixture?
math-m2h-22.commonTrap: Averaging percents and guessing equal volumes ($10$).

rw-craft-01.stem:
The first public demonstration of a telephone in 1876 astonished audiences who had never heard a voice travel by wire. Yet astonishment alone did not secure the device's future. Investors still needed proof that the telephone could move from spectacle to daily utility—proof that arrived only when exchanges linked households and businesses into a working network.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence ("Yet astonishment alone did not secure the device's future.") in the text as a whole?

[Treat the second sentence as the underlined sentence.]

choices.A: It introduces a counterexample that disproves the usefulness of telephones.
choices.B: It qualifies the opening emphasis on public amazement by shifting focus to a remaining practical obstacle.
choices.C: It summarizes the entire history of electrical invention in the nineteenth century.
choices.D: It provides a definition of the word "exchange."

rw-craft-01.explanation: The opening stresses astonishment; "Yet" signals a turn: amazement wasn't enough—utility/network proof was still needed. That is a qualifying shift, not a disproof (A), not a full-history summary (C), and not a definition (D).
rw-craft-01.method: Function of a turn sentence: contrast word (Yet) + what changes in focus.
rw-craft-01.speedTip: Circle contrast words; ask what the sentence does to the prior claim.
rw-craft-01.commonTrap: Reading a qualifier as a total rejection ("disproves") of the opening idea.
rw-craft-01.trap: Reading a qualifier as a total rejection ("disproves") of the opening idea.

rw-craft-02.stem:
Marine biologists once treated coral reefs primarily as colorful tourist destinations. A generation of research has since reframed reefs as living infrastructure: they buffer shorelines, host fisheries, and store carbon in their skeletons. That reframing has, in turn, changed which restoration projects governments choose to fund.

The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.A: argue that tourism to coral reefs should be banned.
choices.B: explain how a changed scientific framing of reefs has influenced conservation funding priorities.
choices.C: list every species that inhabit coral reefs.

rw-craft-02.explanation: The passage moves from old framing → new "living infrastructure" framing → funding consequences. B captures that purpose. A invents a ban. C overclaims completeness. D falsely denies tourism mentioned as the old view.
rw-craft-02.method: Purpose ≈ overall arc, not one detail.
rw-craft-02.speedTip: Track beginning→shift→consequence; that arc is usually the purpose.
rw-craft-02.commonTrap: Elevating a side detail (tourism) into the author's main aim.
rw-craft-02.trap: Elevating a side detail (tourism) into the author's main aim.

rw-craft-03.stem:
Critics of the new downtown plaza claimed it would empty adjacent shops by drawing pedestrians into a single open square. Early sales data suggest otherwise: shops facing the plaza saw weekend foot traffic rise, and several storefronts that had been vacant for months signed leases within a year. The plaza, it seems, concentrated attention without starving its neighbors.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: A prediction is presented, then evidence is offered that challenges that prediction, followed by a brief interpretive conclusion.
choices.B: A scientific experiment is described in chronological order.
choices.C: Two architectural styles are compared feature by feature.
choices.D: A biography of a city planner is narrated from birth to retirement.

rw-craft-03.explanation: Claim/prediction (empty shops) → contrary data (traffic/leases) → interpretive wrap ("concentrated attention..."). That matches A. No experiment chronology, style comparison, or biography.
rw-craft-03.speedTip: Structure answers should mirror the passage's actual moves, not its topic.
rw-craft-03.commonTrap: Picking a familiar structure template (biography, experiment) unrelated to the text's moves.
rw-craft-03.trap: Picking a familiar structure template (biography, experiment) unrelated to the text's moves.

rw-craft-04.stem:
"We do not claim that bilingual education is a cure-all," the report states, "only that students with sustained support in both languages showed stronger reading gains than matched peers in English-only programs." The authors then detail sample sizes, assessment tools, and limitations of their quasi-experimental design.

In context, the quotation primarily serves to

choices.A: dismiss all English-only programs as worthless.
choices.B: narrow the report's claim and avoid an overstated conclusion before presenting methods.
choices.C: introduce a personal anecdote about learning a second language.
choices.D: argue that reading gains are impossible without bilingual education.

rw-craft-04.explanation: "Not a cure-all" / "only that..." deliberately limits the claim before methods—B. A and D exaggerate beyond the measured comparison. C invents an anecdote.
rw-craft-04.method: Quotes that say "not X, only Y" usually qualify/limit.
rw-craft-04.speedTip: Precise verbs: qualify, limit, concede—not dismiss or prove.
rw-craft-04.commonTrap: Treating a careful limitation as an extreme attack on the opposing approach.
rw-craft-04.trap: Treating a careful limitation as an extreme attack on the opposing approach.

rw-craft-05.stem:
In the 1930s, documentary photographers working for government agencies produced stark images of drought and displacement. Those photographs did more than record suffering; they trained urban viewers to see rural crisis as a national, not merely regional, problem. Later magazine spreads borrowed the same visual grammar when covering other disasters.

What is the main purpose of the second sentence in the text?

choices.A: To concede that the photographs were artistically unsuccessful.
choices.B: To specify an effect of the photographs beyond mere documentation.
choices.C: To list the names of individual photographers.
choices.D: To argue that magazines should avoid covering disasters.

rw-craft-05.explanation: "Did more than record..." explicitly expands function from documentation to shaping national perception—B. A contradicts the positive framing. C and D aren't in the sentence.
rw-craft-05.method: "More than X; they Y" pattern = expand function beyond the obvious.
rw-craft-05.speedTip: Purpose of a middle sentence is often to deepen or specify the prior claim.
rw-craft-05.commonTrap: Missing the "more than record" cue and inventing criticism or policy advice.
rw-craft-05.trap: Missing the "more than record" cue and inventing criticism or policy advice.

rw-craft-06.stem:
Most accounts of the silk trade emphasize caravans moving east to west. Less often discussed is the reverse flow of techniques: glassmaking knowledge, for example, traveled toward production centers that already excelled in textiles. Mapping those westward-to-eastward transfers complicates any story that treats Silk Road exchange as a one-way delivery of Asian goods to Europe.

The author uses the example of glassmaking knowledge primarily to

choices.A: illustrate that cultural and technical exchange along trade routes was not exclusively unidirectional.
choices.B: prove that silk was never traded along the Silk Road.
choices.C: argue that glass is more valuable than silk.
choices.D: describe modern factory methods for making glass.

rw-craft-06.explanation: Glassmaking is a concrete reverse-flow example that challenges one-way narratives—A. B denies silk trade absurdly. C invents a value ranking. D invents modern factories.
rw-craft-06.method: Examples usually illustrate the abstract claim nearby (here: reverse flow / not one-way).
rw-craft-06.speedTip: Ask: what claim is this example serving?
rw-craft-06.commonTrap: Treating an illustrative example as a denial of the main trade good.
rw-craft-06.trap: Treating an illustrative example as a denial of the main trade good.

rw-craft-07.stem:
The museum's new audio guide offers three tracks for each painting: a two-minute overview, a curator deep dive, and a children's story version. Visitors who sampled more than one track stayed longer at each stop, according to sensors in the gallery floor. Still, some educators worry that constant headphone use isolates viewers from conversation.

Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?

choices.A: It introduces a lingering concern that qualifies the positive finding about dwell time.
choices.B: It restates the audio guide's three track options.
choices.C: It proves that sensors in gallery floors are inaccurate.
choices.D: It provides a biography of the museum's director.

rw-craft-07.explanation: "Still" flags a concern (isolation) that qualifies the upbeat dwell-time result—A. B repeats earlier content (it doesn't). C and D invent attacks/biography.
rw-craft-07.method: Final "Still/However" sentences often qualify or complicate prior success.
rw-craft-07.speedTip: Contrast opener + new worry = qualify, not erase, the prior point.
rw-craft-07.commonTrap: Reading a qualifying concern as proof that the data are false.
rw-craft-07.trap: Reading a qualifying concern as proof that the data are false.

rw-craft-08.stem:
If renewable energy were only a matter of generating electricity, the transition would already look nearly complete in some regions. The harder problem is reliability when the wind drops and the sun sets. Until affordable storage and flexible demand catch up, grids must still lean on backup sources that reformers would prefer to retire.

Which choice best describes the structure of the text?

choices.A: It defines a term, then lists unrelated historical dates.
choices.B: It presents an optimistic premise, then identifies a remaining obstacle and its temporary consequence.
choices.C: It narrates a single inventor's career from childhood onward.
choices.D: It compares two novels' plots in chronological order.

rw-craft-08.explanation: Optimistic premise (generation nearly complete) → harder problem (reliability/storage) → interim consequence (backup sources)—B. Other options don't match content.
rw-craft-08.method: If/then pivot texts often: seeming success → real bottleneck → implication.
rw-craft-08.speedTip: Match structure labels to actual sentence jobs.
rw-craft-08.commonTrap: Choosing biography/novel templates because they sound "structural."
rw-craft-08.trap: Choosing biography/novel templates because they sound "structural."

rw-craft-09.stem:
Early reviewers praised the novel's plot twists but barely mentioned its quieter achievement: the way ordinary mealtime conversations reveal class tensions without a single speech about inequality. Those kitchen-table scenes do the novel's real political work.

The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.A: summarize every plot twist in the novel.
choices.B: contend that reviewers overlooked a subtler means by which the novel addresses class.
choices.C: argue that novels should never include plot twists.
choices.D: provide nutritional advice related to mealtimes.

rw-craft-09.explanation: The author contrasts praised twists with neglected mealtime scenes that handle class—purpose is to highlight what reviewers missed—B. A overfocuses on twists. C and D are off-topic.
rw-craft-09.method: Purpose often = author's corrective emphasis (what others missed).
rw-craft-09.speedTip: Look for contrast between common praise and author's preferred focus.
rw-craft-09.commonTrap: Mistaking the author's topic (class scenes) for a demand to abolish plot twists.
rw-craft-09.trap: Mistaking the author's topic (class scenes) for a demand to abolish plot twists.

rw-craft-10.stem:
"Granted, the sample includes only coastal cities," the sociologist writes, "so inland patterns may differ." She nevertheless argues that the coastal findings are robust enough to guide waterfront zoning debates where flooding risk is already documented.

The underlined sentence ("Granted, the sample includes only coastal cities, so inland patterns may differ.") primarily serves to

choices.B: concede a limitation in scope before reaffirming a narrower claim about coastal applications.
choices.C: introduce unrelated data about mountain towns.

rw-craft-10.explanation: "Granted" signals concession of a scope limit, then "nevertheless" keeps a narrower coastal claim—B. A overreads concession as total abandonment. C and D aren't present.
rw-craft-10.speedTip: Concession ≠ full retreat when a limited claim follows.
rw-craft-10.commonTrap: Treating any admission of limitation as a total withdrawal of the argument.
rw-craft-10.trap: Treating any admission of limitation as a total withdrawal of the argument.

rw-craft-11.stem:
Consider the honeybee, which dances to share the location of nectar. Now consider the leafcutter ant, which cannot dance a map but builds fungus gardens with a division of labor rivaling a factory. Both societies complicate the assumption that complex cooperation requires human-like language.

The author mentions leafcutter ants primarily to

choices.A: provide a second example that broadens the challenge to a language-based view of complex cooperation.
choices.B: argue that bees are not social insects.
choices.C: explain how to keep ants as pets.
choices.D: deny that bees communicate at all.

rw-craft-11.explanation: Bee example first; ant example extends the same challenge to cooperation-without-human-language—A. B and D contradict the passage. C invents pet advice.
rw-craft-11.method: "Now consider" often adds a parallel example to widen the claim.
rw-craft-11.speedTip: Second examples usually reinforce/broaden, not cancel, the first.
rw-craft-11.commonTrap: Reading a parallel example as a rejection of the first organism discussed.
rw-craft-11.trap: Reading a parallel example as a rejection of the first organism discussed.

rw-craft-12.stem:
City planners promised that removing the elevated highway would reunite neighborhoods long split by concrete. What they did not advertise—and what residents soon noticed—was a temporary surge in surface-street congestion during demolition. The long-term reconnection was real; the short-term inconvenience was underplayed.

Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text?

choices.A: It supplies a definition of "elevated highway."
choices.B: It introduces an omitted short-term cost that complicates the planners' upbeat promise.
choices.C: It proves that reconnection never occurred.
choices.D: It lists construction materials used in demolition.

rw-craft-12.explanation: "What they did not advertise" reveals an omitted downside (congestion), complicating the promise—B. A/D aren't there. C conflicts with "long-term reconnection was real."
rw-craft-12.method: Function = reveal omitted cost / complicate promise.
rw-craft-12.speedTip: Sentences about what was "not advertised" usually add a caveat.
rw-craft-12.commonTrap: Using a temporary cost to claim the long-term benefit never happened.
rw-craft-12.trap: Using a temporary cost to claim the long-term benefit never happened.

rw-craft-13.stem:
Textbook timelines present the Scientific Revolution as a clean break from medieval thought. Historians of science increasingly reject that drama. They trace experimental practices and mathematical tools across centuries, showing continuity where older narratives insisted on rupture.

The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.A: defend the textbook timeline as fully accurate.
choices.B: characterize a scholarly shift away from rupture narratives toward continuity in the history of science.
choices.D: argue that mathematics is unimportant to science.

rw-craft-13.explanation: Textbooks = rupture; historians = continuity across centuries. Purpose is to characterize that scholarly shift—B. A reverses the stance. C and D are unsupported.
rw-craft-13.method: Purpose tracks the author's stance toward competing narratives.
rw-craft-13.speedTip: When A says X and B rejects X for Y, purpose is often "characterize the shift."
rw-craft-13.commonTrap: Aligning with the textbook view the passage is distancing itself from.
rw-craft-13.trap: Aligning with the textbook view the passage is distancing itself from.

rw-craft-14.stem:
The opening chapter floods the reader with technical names for cloud types. Only afterward does the memoirist admit she learned those names during a single summer of grief, when naming the sky became a way to keep walking. The catalogue, then, was never neutral meteorology.

In context, the final sentence primarily serves to

choices.A: reinterpret the earlier list of cloud names as emotionally motivated rather than purely technical.
choices.B: correct factual errors in cloud classification.
choices.C: urge readers to become professional meteorologists.

rw-craft-14.explanation: "Then" + "never neutral" reinterprets the cloud catalogue in light of grief—A. B/C/D invent corrections, career advice, or climate stats.
rw-craft-14.method: Late sentences often reframe what came before.
rw-craft-14.commonTrap: Taking a memoir reframing as a science-fact correction.
rw-craft-14.trap: Taking a memoir reframing as a science-fact correction.

rw-craft-15.stem:
Proponents call the policy a "nudge" toward healthier cafeteria choices. Opponents call the same policy "paternalism in a lunch line." The labels matter: each frames student autonomy differently before any calorie data are discussed.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It recounts a scientific discovery in strict chronological order.
choices.B: It juxtaposes two competing labels for a policy and then explains why the labeling conflict is consequential.
choices.C: It provides a recipe for cafeteria food.
choices.D: It presents a statistical table of calorie counts.

rw-craft-15.explanation: Two labels → why labels matter for framing autonomy—B. No discovery chronology, recipe, or table.
rw-craft-15.method: Structure = juxtapose terms → state stakes of naming.
rw-craft-15.speedTip: If the passage is about words/labels, the structure answer usually mentions framing.
rw-craft-15.commonTrap: Forcing a chronology/data structure onto a framing-focused paragraph.
rw-craft-15.trap: Forcing a chronology/data structure onto a framing-focused paragraph.

rw-craft-16.stem:
It is tempting to treat the archive as a transparent window onto the past. In practice, archivists' cataloging choices—what is indexed, what is left in unlabeled boxes—shape which stories researchers can easily tell. Silence in the record is sometimes an accident of storage, not evidence that nothing happened.

The author discusses archivists' cataloging choices primarily to

choices.A: illustrate that access to the past is mediated by present institutional decisions.
choices.B: argue that all archives should be destroyed.
choices.C: prove that historical events never occurred.
choices.D: describe the architecture of a particular library building.

rw-craft-16.explanation: Cataloging choices show mediation of access—A. B/C are extreme distortions. D invents architecture.
rw-craft-16.method: Examples after "tempting to treat X as transparent" usually expose mediation/limits.
rw-craft-16.speedTip: Match example to the abstract warning in the first sentence.
rw-craft-16.commonTrap: Escalating a point about mediation into "destroy archives" or "nothing happened."
rw-craft-16.trap: Escalating a point about mediation into "destroy archives" or "nothing happened."

rw-craft-17.stem:
