The composer's early quartets follow textbook sonata form with almost stubborn clarity. Her late quartets fracture themes mid-phrase and postpone tonal resolution for pages. Hearing the late works against the early ones makes the experiment audible: she learned the rules thoroughly enough to break them on purpose.

What is the main function of the comparison between early and late quartets?

choices.A: To suggest that the composer never studied music theory.
choices.B: To establish a baseline of formal control against which the late stylistic ruptures can be understood as deliberate.
choices.C: To argue that sonata form is obsolete for all composers.
choices.D: To claim that the late quartets were written first.

rw-craft-17.explanation: Early clarity = baseline; late fractures = intentional experiment once rules were mastered—B. A contradicts "learned the rules." C universalizes. D reverses chronology.
rw-craft-17.method: Early-vs-late comparisons often create a foil for interpreting change as deliberate.
rw-craft-17.speedTip: Ask what the early work helps you notice about the late work.
rw-craft-17.commonTrap: Reading mastery-then-break as ignorance of the rules.
rw-craft-17.trap: Reading mastery-then-break as ignorance of the rules.

rw-craft-18.stem:
A viral chart claims that a single city "solved" traffic by biking alone. Look closer: the chart's timeline starts the year a major subway line opened, omits population decline in the urban core, and uses a nonstandard definition of "delay." Charts can persuade by what they leave out.

The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.A: encourage cities to eliminate all subway construction.
choices.B: caution readers that selective presentation can make a chart overstate a single cause.
choices.C: prove that biking never reduces traffic.
choices.D: celebrate the viral chart as a model of transparency.

rw-craft-18.explanation: The text exposes omissions/nonstandard definitions to warn about overstated single-cause claims—B. A invents anti-subway advocacy. C overclaims. D contradicts the critical stance.
rw-craft-18.method: Purpose of "look closer / leave out" passages is usually caution about evidence quality.
rw-craft-18.speedTip: Author attitude: skeptical of the viral claim, not of bikes in general.
rw-craft-18.commonTrap: Turning a critique of chart rhetoric into a blanket anti-biking conclusion.
rw-craft-18.trap: Turning a critique of chart rhetoric into a blanket anti-biking conclusion.

rw-craft-19.stem:
"Not every migrant journey ends in arrival," the historian notes, before turning to ship manifests that list passengers who died in transit. Those names, she argues, belong in narratives of migration as surely as the names of those who disembarked.

In the text, the historian's statement ("Not every migrant journey ends in arrival") primarily serves to

choices.A: introduce a corrective focus on in-transit deaths often omitted from arrival-centered migration stories.
choices.B: deny that any migrants ever arrived.
choices.C: provide a shipping company's financial report.

rw-craft-19.explanation: The line opens space for deaths in transit as part of migration history—A. B overreads "not every" as "none." C/D are irrelevant.
rw-craft-19.method: "Not every X" often opens a neglected category the author will center next.
rw-craft-19.speedTip: Expect the next sentence to exemplify the neglected category.
rw-craft-19.commonTrap: Misreading a partial negative ("not every") as a universal negative.
rw-craft-19.trap: Misreading a partial negative ("not every") as a universal negative.

rw-craft-20.stem:
First the drought emptied the reservoir. Then water-intensive factories closed. Only later did census figures show younger workers leaving the county. Local leaders who blamed "a sudden labor shortage" reversed the causal order: the shortage was a late symptom, not the originating shock.

Which choice best describes the structure of the text?

choices.A: It lists unrelated tourist attractions in the county.
choices.B: It sequences cascading effects and then critiques leaders for mistaking a late symptom for the root cause.
choices.C: It presents a controlled laboratory experiment with a placebo group.
choices.D: It offers a balanced debate with equal space for two opposing economic theories.

rw-craft-20.explanation: Drought → factory closures → out-migration, then critique of leaders' reversed causal story—B. A/C/D don't match.
rw-craft-20.method: "First...Then...Only later..." signals sequenced effects; the ending evaluates a misreading of that sequence.
rw-craft-20.speedTip: Causal-order critiques often end by naming the mistake (symptom vs. root).
rw-craft-20.commonTrap: Calling a one-sided critique of leaders a "balanced debate."
rw-craft-20.trap: Calling a one-sided critique of leaders a "balanced debate."

rw-form-01.stem: The collection of essays on climate migration ____ scheduled to appear next spring under a university press imprint.
rw-form-01.explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'collection,' not 'essays.' Singular subject takes 'is.' A, B, and C wrongly agree with the nearer plural noun.
rw-form-01.method: Cross out the prepositional phrase 'of essays on climate migration.' Match the verb to 'collection.'
rw-form-01.speedTip: Of-phrase distractors: verb agrees with the head noun before 'of.'

rw-form-02.stem: Neither the conductor nor the principal violinists ____ willing to shorten the cadenza for the radio broadcast.
rw-form-02.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Violinists' is plural, so 'were' is correct. A, B, and D are singular forms agreeing with 'conductor' instead.
rw-form-02.method: For neither X nor Y, check number of Y only. Here Y = violinists (plural).
rw-form-02.speedTip: Neither/nor and either/or → agree with the noun closest to the verb.

choices.A: rare shorebirds could be seen by the students
choices.B: the students could see rare shorebirds
choices.C: rare shorebirds were visible to the students
choices.D: seeing rare shorebirds was possible for the students

rw-form-03.explanation: The opening modifier 'Walking...' must modify the students who walk. B places 'the students' as the subject. A, C, and D create dangling modifiers implying shorebirds or 'seeing' were walking.
rw-form-03.method: After an -ing opener, the noun right after the comma must be the doer of that -ing action.
rw-form-03.speedTip: Opening -ing phrase → subject after comma = who is doing it.

rw-form-04.stem: By the time the panel convened, the researchers ____ their preliminary findings to three peer reviewers.
rw-form-04.explanation: Past perfect 'had submitted' correctly places the submission before another past event ('convened'). A and D are present; B (present perfect) doesn't clearly sequence two past events.
rw-form-04.method: Two past times: earlier action → had + past participle; later past → simple past.
rw-form-04.speedTip: By the time + past → earlier action usually needs had + V3.

rw-form-05.stem: After reviewing the applications, the committee announced ____ decision to fund two community arts projects.
rw-form-05.explanation: A collective noun acting as one unit ('committee announced [one] decision') takes singular 'its.' A wrongly treats the committee as plural individuals here; C is a contraction of 'it is'; D is the wrong word.
rw-form-05.method: Decide if the collective acts as one unit. One decision → its.

rw-form-06.stem: The internship requires students to draft headlines, pitch story ideas, and ____ finished articles before the evening deadline.
rw-form-06.explanation: Parallelism with 'to draft... pitch... and edit' (bare infinitives after 'requires students to' with later bare forms) — actually the structure is 'requires students to X, Y, and Z' so all should be infinitive/base: draft, pitch, and edit. A and D break form; B repeats 'to' unnecessarily and is less parallel with bare 'draft/pitch' if those are bare—wait, draft and pitch are bare after 'to' applies to first only... 'to draft, pitch, and edit' is standard parallel. C matches.
rw-form-06.method: List after 'to': keep the same verb form for each item.
rw-form-06.speedTip: Parallel list: match verb shapes—edit, not 'the editing of.'

rw-form-07.stem: Among the archives' most fragile items ____ a hand-painted map of the estuary from 1789.
rw-form-07.explanation: Inverted sentence: true subject is singular 'map.' Use 'is.' Plural verbs wrongly agree with 'items.'
rw-form-07.method: In 'Among... lies/is X,' find X after the verb and match number.
rw-form-07.speedTip: Inverted 'Among/Here/There' sentences: subject often comes after the verb.

rw-form-08.stem: The sculptor preferred working with reclaimed metal, which ____ both durability and an irregular surface texture.
rw-form-08.explanation: 'Which' refers to 'reclaimed metal' (singular), so 'offers' is correct. A and D are plural; C is an awkward progressive.
rw-form-08.method: Find the antecedent of which/that. Match verb to that noun's number.
rw-form-08.speedTip: Which/that verb agrees with the noun it renames—not with a nearby plural.

rw-form-09.stem: Critics praised the director for her precise pacing, inventive camera angles, and ____.

choices.A: how she cast the supporting roles carefully
choices.B: careful casting of the supporting roles
choices.C: she cast the supporting roles carefully
choices.D: to cast the supporting roles carefully

rw-form-09.explanation: The list is of noun phrases (pacing, angles, casting). B keeps that parallel structure. A, C, and D shift into clauses or infinitives.
rw-form-09.method: Identify the pattern of the first two list items; force the third to match grammatically.
rw-form-09.speedTip: Noun, noun, and noun—don't switch to a clause mid-list.

rw-form-10.stem: If the laboratory ____ additional funding last year, it could have expanded the field survey.
rw-form-10.explanation: Counterfactual past condition uses past perfect in the if-clause ('had received') with 'could have' in the result. A is simple past; C and D are wrong time frames.
rw-form-10.method: Spot 'could have' / 'would have' in the result → if-clause wants had + V3.
rw-form-10.speedTip: If... had + V3, ... would/could have + V3.

rw-form-11.stem: Readers often disagree with the columnist, but few can deny that ____ arguments are carefully researched.
rw-form-11.explanation: Before the noun 'arguments,' you need the possessive adjective 'her.' 'Hers' stands alone; 'she' is subject case; 'herself' is reflexive.
rw-form-11.method: Blank before a noun → possessive determiner (her/their/its), not hers/them.

rw-form-12.stem: Measured against last decade's baseline, the wetlands ____ a 22 percent increase in nesting pairs.
rw-form-12.explanation: Plural subject 'wetlands' takes 'have shown.' A and B are singular; D is not a finite verb.
rw-form-12.method: Ignore the opener; identify subject 'wetlands' and pick plural verb.
rw-form-12.speedTip: Don't let an introductory phrase hide a plural subject.

rw-form-13.stem: The professor asked Liam and ____ to present the conflicting interpretations side by side.
rw-form-13.explanation: Object of 'asked' needs object case: 'Liam and me.' A is subject case; B reflexive has no separate antecedent needing emphasis; D is possessive.
rw-form-13.method: Remove 'Liam and' and test: 'asked me to present,' not 'asked I.'
rw-form-13.speedTip: Drop the other name; whatever case remains is correct.

rw-form-14.stem: Published in serial form between 1852 and 1853, ____.

choices.A: readers eagerly awaited each new installment of the novel
choices.B: the novel's readers awaited each installment eagerly
choices.C: each new installment of the novel was awaited by readers
choices.D: the novel attracted readers who awaited each installment

rw-form-14.explanation: The opening participle 'Published...' must modify the novel. D correctly makes 'the novel' the subject. A/B make readers published; C makes 'installment' published.
rw-form-14.method: Participle opener modifies the noun right after the comma—pick the option where that noun is logically publishable.
rw-form-14.speedTip: Published/Written/Found + comma → next noun = the thing published.

rw-form-15.stem: Every one of the recovered manuscripts ____ annotations in at least two distinct hands.
rw-form-15.explanation: 'Every one' is singular, so 'contains' agrees. Plural verbs agree wrongly with 'manuscripts.'
rw-form-15.method: Cross out 'of the recovered manuscripts.' Subject = Every one → singular verb.
rw-form-15.speedTip: Every/Each + of + plurals → still singular verb.

rw-form-16.stem: The twin lenses of the instrument ____ the image before it reaches the sensor.
rw-form-16.explanation: Plural subject 'lenses' takes 'focus.' Singular forms agree with 'instrument' by mistake.
rw-form-16.method: Subject is 'lenses,' not 'instrument' in the of-phrase.

rw-form-17.stem: For accuracy, the report relies on court transcripts rather than ____.

choices.A: what was remembered by witnesses years later

rw-form-17.explanation: Parallelism: 'court transcripts' (noun phrase) pairs best with 'witnesses' later memories' (noun phrase). A/D are clauses; C is an awkward gerund phrase.
rw-form-17.method: 'Rather than' sets up a parallel contrast—match grammatical form to the first item.
rw-form-17.speedTip: Rather than/as well as → keep both sides the same part of speech.

rw-form-18.stem: The artists' collective has opened ____ first gallery in the warehouse district.
rw-form-18.explanation: Collective 'collective' acting as one organization takes 'its.' A is plural; B and D are contractions.
rw-form-18.method: One gallery opening by one group entity → its.
rw-form-18.speedTip: Its = possessive; it's = it is—never confuse on possessives.

rw-form-19.stem: While ____ the ancient frescoes, a faint earlier sketch became visible beneath the paint.
rw-form-19.explanation: The main clause subject is 'sketch,' which cannot be cleaning. Only A supplies an explicit logical subject for the while-clause. B, C, and D create dangling or ambiguous modifiers implying the sketch was cleaning.
rw-form-19.method: If the main subject can't do the while-action, the while-clause needs its own clear subject (full clause).
rw-form-19.speedTip: While -ing + comma + inanimate subject = dangler—use a full while-clause instead.

rw-form-20.stem: Data from the coastal buoys ____ that average wave height has increased since 1995.
rw-form-20.explanation: 'Data' is treated as plural in formal SAT-style usage here with plural verb 'indicate.' B and D are singular; C is not a finite verb. (Some style guides allow singular data; on these items, match the intended plural academic convention when plural verb is the keyed choice.)
rw-form-20.method: In Digital SAT conventions items, 'data' typically takes a plural verb when that option is present and others are singular mismatches.
rw-form-20.speedTip: Academic 'data' → often plural verb on the SAT.

rw-form-21.stem: The board will discuss the proposal that the campus ____ later weekend library hours during finals.
rw-form-21.explanation: After a recommendation/proposal that..., English uses the subjunctive base form: 'that the campus offer.' A indicative; C past; D progressive.
rw-form-21.method: Trigger words: propose/recommend/insist/demand that → base verb (offer, not offers).

rw-form-22.stem: Maya Angelou's memoirs, together with her poetry collections, ____ a vivid record of twentieth-century American life.
rw-form-22.explanation: The subject is plural 'memoirs'; the 'together with...' phrase does not change the number. B and D are singular; C is nonfinite.
rw-form-22.method: Cross out 'together with her poetry collections.' Memoirs → plural verb.
rw-form-22.speedTip: Together with/as well as/along with → doesn't make subject plural or singular; ignore it.

rw-form-23.stem: The two ____ approaches differed mainly in how they treated missing survey responses.
rw-form-23.explanation: Plural owners (two statisticians) sharing approaches take statisticians' (apostrophe after s). A is plural noun not possessive; B is singular possessive; D is nonstandard.
rw-form-23.method: Plural noun ending in s → add only an apostrophe for possessive.

rw-form-24.stem: Since 2018, the foundation ____ scholarships to students pursuing conservation biology.
rw-form-24.explanation: 'Since 2018' signals an action continuing from past to present → present perfect 'has awarded.' A simple past cuts the connection to now; C past perfect needs another past anchor; D simple present is weaker with 'since.'
rw-form-24.method: Since/for + time span up to now → has/have + V3.
rw-form-24.speedTip: Since + year → present perfect, not simple past.

rw-form-25.stem: To reduce glare without darkening the room, the architects installed louvers designed ____ sunlight while admitting diffuse light.
rw-form-25.explanation: 'Designed to + infinitive' is the standard idiom. B is less idiomatic after 'designed'; C is wordy/ungrammatical here; D is awkward.
rw-form-25.method: Remember common patterns: designed to, intended to, required to + base verb.

rw-inf-01.stem:
When the city replaced a congested four-lane road with a two-lane road plus a protected bike lane, average car commute times on that corridor rose by only two minutes, while bike ridership tripled and reported traffic injuries fell by 30%. Nearby merchants had feared lost customers, but monthly sales tax receipts on the corridor held steady.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

A local transportation planner reviewing these results would most likely conclude that

choices.A: protected bike lanes always eliminate car traffic delays in dense cities.
choices.B: the corridor redesign traded a small increase in car travel time for higher bike use and fewer injuries without clear harm to corridor retail sales.
choices.C: merchants on the corridor experienced large revenue losses that sales tax data failed to capture.
choices.D: ridership tripled solely because gasoline prices rose during the same period.

rw-inf-01.explanation: The passage supports a modest car-time increase, big bike/injury gains, and steady sales—exactly B. A overclaims "always eliminate" delays (times rose slightly). C contradicts steady receipts. D invents a gas-price cause not mentioned.
rw-inf-01.method: Inference = combine stated results without adding causes or absolutes.
rw-inf-01.commonTrap: Absolute generalizations or inventing an unstated alternative cause (gas prices).
rw-inf-01.trap: Absolute generalizations or inventing an unstated alternative cause (gas prices).

rw-inf-02.stem:
Archaeologists excavating a coastal settlement found fishhooks made from both local shell and imported bone in the same household trash layers dated to a single generation. Isotope tests show the bone came from inland mammals hunted more than 200 kilometers away. No wheeled vehicles are attested for that culture.

Based on the text, which conclusion is best supported?

choices.A: Every household in the settlement specialized in long-distance trade.
choices.B: People at the settlement had access to materials—or to exchange networks—that connected the coast with inland hunting regions within a relatively short historical window.
choices.C: Inland hunters regularly visited the coast using wheeled carts.
choices.D: Shell fishhooks were inferior to bone fishhooks and were quickly abandoned.

rw-inf-02.explanation: Mixed local and distant materials in the same generation imply coastal–inland connections via access or exchange. A overstates "every household" and "specialized." C invents wheeled carts the text says are unattested. D invents a quality ranking and abandonment not stated.
rw-inf-02.method: Stick to what co-presence of materials implies: connection/access, not universal specialization.
rw-inf-02.speedTip: If the text denies wheeled vehicles, any cart-based inference is dead.
rw-inf-02.commonTrap: Overgeneralizing from one context to "every household" or inventing transport technology.
rw-inf-02.trap: Overgeneralizing from one context to "every household" or inventing transport technology.

rw-inf-03.stem:
In laboratory trials, seedlings grown in soil inoculated with a native mycorrhizal fungus developed deeper root systems and survived drought simulation at higher rates than seedlings in sterile soil. When the same fungus was paired with a non-native tree species, root depth and drought survival did not differ from sterile controls.

What does the text most strongly support?

choices.A: The fungus improves drought resilience for native seedlings under the tested conditions but does not produce the same benefit for the non-native species tested.
choices.B: All fungi enhance root growth in all tree species.
choices.C: Non-native trees cannot survive drought under any conditions.
choices.D: Sterile soil is preferable for native forestry projects.

rw-inf-03.explanation: Results show a native-species benefit and no benefit for the tested non-native—A captures that limited inference. B and C use unjustified universals. D contradicts the native-seedling results.
rw-inf-03.method: Scope the claim to species actually tested; don't universalize.
rw-inf-03.speedTip: Watch for "all," "any," and policy flips that ignore the positive native result.
rw-inf-03.commonTrap: Turning a species-specific result into a universal rule about all fungi or all trees.
rw-inf-03.trap: Turning a species-specific result into a universal rule about all fungi or all trees.

rw-inf-04.stem:
During the 1890s, several U.S. cities opened free evening lecture series in public libraries. Attendance logs show large crowds for talks on electricity and sanitation, while lectures on classical poetry drew far fewer listeners. Library purchasing records from the same years show spikes in books related to applied science after the popular lectures.

Which inference is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Classical poetry had no audience anywhere in the 1890s.
choices.B: Public interest in practical scientific topics, as reflected in lecture attendance, coincided with increased borrowing or acquisition of related applied-science books.
choices.C: Library patrons attended electricity lectures only to socialize.
choices.D: Sanitation lectures caused cities to rebuild their sewer systems immediately.

rw-inf-04.explanation: Crowds for applied topics plus purchasing spikes for related books support a coincidence of interest reflected in both attendance and acquisitions. A is extreme and unsupported. C invents motive. D leaps from lectures to immediate citywide rebuilding.
rw-inf-04.method: Connect the two data streams (attendance + purchasing) without inventing motives or city actions.
rw-inf-04.speedTip: Causal leaps to municipal construction are too strong for attendance logs.
rw-inf-04.commonTrap: Inferring grand civic outcomes or zero audience for poetry from comparative attendance.
rw-inf-04.trap: Inferring grand civic outcomes or zero audience for poetry from comparative attendance.

rw-inf-05.stem:
A theater company staged the same new play in a 99-seat black-box theater and, later, in a 500-seat proscenium house. Critics praised intimate audience–actor proximity in the small theater; in the large house, several reviewers said emotional climaxes "felt distant." Ticket sales per available seat were higher in the black-box run.

Based on the text, which choice is best supported?

choices.A: The play cannot succeed in any venue larger than 99 seats.
choices.B: For this production, the smaller venue's intimacy aligned with more favorable critical comments about emotional impact and stronger seat-fill rates than the larger house run.
choices.D: Critics disliked the script itself rather than the staging conditions.

rw-inf-05.explanation: B stays within the comparison given: intimacy praised, climaxes "distant" in the large house, better fill rate in the small theater. A and C are absolute industry claims. D contradicts reviewers' focus on distance/proximity.
rw-inf-05.method: Keep the inference tied to this play/production and the two venues.
rw-inf-05.speedTip: Eliminate answers that ban entire venue types.
rw-inf-05.commonTrap: Overgeneralizing one production's venue contrast into a rule about all large theaters.
rw-inf-05.trap: Overgeneralizing one production's venue contrast into a rule about all large theaters.

rw-inf-06.stem:
Satellite measurements show that nighttime light intensity in a rapidly growing tech corridor increased 60% from 2010 to 2020. Ground surveys in the same years show that median household income rose and that the share of agricultural land converted to commercial use roughly doubled. Bird counts for several grassland species in remnant fields declined.

Which conclusion is most reasonable?

choices.A: Nighttime lights directly poisoned grassland birds.
choices.B: The corridor's economic and land-use transformation—marked by brighter nights, higher incomes, and farmland conversion—occurred alongside declines in some grassland bird counts.
choices.C: Grassland birds increased in urban centers even as they declined in remnant fields.
choices.D: Median income rose only because agricultural jobs disappeared.

rw-inf-06.explanation: B accurately bundles co-occurring trends without asserting a single proven mechanism. A invents poisoning. C invents urban bird increases. D asserts a sole cause for income growth.
rw-inf-06.speedTip: Reject medical-sounding mechanisms (poison) not in the text.
rw-inf-06.commonTrap: Forcing a specific causal mechanism when the passage only shows concurrent trends.
rw-inf-06.trap: Forcing a specific causal mechanism when the passage only shows concurrent trends.

rw-inf-07.stem:
In a randomized trial, adults who took a 20-minute outdoor walk during lunch reported lower afternoon sleepiness scores than adults who spent the same interval scrolling on their phones indoors. Both groups worked similar office jobs and ate comparable lunches.

The results most strongly support the conclusion that

choices.A: any outdoor activity of any length cures sleep disorders.
choices.B: under the trial conditions, a short outdoor walk was associated with less afternoon sleepiness than an equal period of indoor phone use.
choices.C: phone use is the primary cause of all workplace fatigue nationwide.
choices.D: lunch composition has no effect on alertness for any worker.

rw-inf-07.explanation: B restates the controlled comparison precisely. A inflates to "any" activity and "cures disorders." C globalizes phone use as primary cause. D overclaims from "comparable lunches" to "no effect ever."
rw-inf-07.method: Match inference strength to study scope: this walk vs. this control.
rw-inf-07.speedTip: "Cures," "primary cause of all," and "no effect for any" are almost never supported.
rw-inf-07.commonTrap: Inflating a relative alertness finding into medical cure or nationwide causation claims.
rw-inf-07.trap: Inflating a relative alertness finding into medical cure or nationwide causation claims.

rw-inf-08.stem:
Medieval account books from a Flemish cloth guild list payments to women for spinning and finishing work in nearly every year of a 40-year span, yet official guild membership rolls from the same period include almost no women's names. Legal statutes barred women from full guild membership but were silent on paid subcontracting.

What is most strongly implied?

choices.A: Women performed no skilled textile labor in Flanders.
choices.B: Women could be economically important to cloth production through paid work even when formal membership rules largely excluded them from guild rolls.
choices.C: Guilds secretly made all women full members.
choices.D: Account books from the period are forgeries.

rw-inf-08.explanation: Persistent payments plus near-absent membership implies labor contribution without formal membership—B. A contradicts payment records. C contradicts rolls and statutes. D is baseless skepticism.
rw-inf-08.method: Reconcile the tension: paid work yes, membership no → economic role without formal status.
rw-inf-08.speedTip: Don't "resolve" a documentary tension by calling sources forged.
rw-inf-08.commonTrap: Denying women's labor entirely or inventing secret membership to erase the contradiction.
rw-inf-08.trap: Denying women's labor entirely or inventing secret membership to erase the contradiction.

rw-inf-09.stem:
A streaming platform tested two homepage layouts. Layout A emphasized personalized recommendations; Layout B emphasized trending titles. Users on Layout A watched more total minutes but started fewer new titles per week; users on Layout B sampled more titles but watched fewer minutes per title on average.

Which inference is best supported?

choices.A: Layout A is objectively better for every business metric.
choices.B: The layouts appear to encourage different viewing patterns: deeper watching of fewer titles versus broader sampling with less time per title.

rw-inf-09.explanation: The data describe complementary patterns—more minutes/fewer new titles vs. more sampling/less time per title—captured by B. A ignores the tradeoff. C invents dislike. D contradicts more total minutes on A.
rw-inf-09.method: Describe the tradeoff; don't declare a single winner.
rw-inf-09.speedTip: If both layouts "win" on different metrics, the answer is usually about different patterns.
rw-inf-09.commonTrap: Collapsing a tradeoff into "A is better on every metric."
rw-inf-09.trap: Collapsing a tradeoff into "A is better on every metric."

rw-inf-10.stem:
Chemists comparing two battery electrolytes found that Electrolyte R remained stable after 500 charge cycles at high temperature, whereas Electrolyte S degraded and lost 40% capacity under the same protocol. Electrolyte R costs about twice as much to synthesize at laboratory scale.

Based on the text, which statement is most supportable?

choices.A: Electrolyte R is already cheaper than S for commercial mass production.
choices.B: Under the tested high-temperature cycling conditions, R preserved capacity far better than S, though R is more expensive to make in the lab.
choices.C: Electrolyte S is unsafe for any consumer device.
choices.D: Cost is irrelevant to electrolyte choice.

rw-inf-10.explanation: B combines the stability result and the lab cost fact without inventing commercial prices or safety bans. A invents mass-production cost. C invents safety. D contradicts the text's inclusion of cost as a relevant detail.
rw-inf-10.method: Report tested performance + stated cost; don't extrapolate to factories or bans.
rw-inf-10.commonTrap: Conflating laboratory synthesis cost with commercial pricing or inventing safety failures.
rw-inf-10.trap: Conflating laboratory synthesis cost with commercial pricing or inventing safety failures.

rw-inf-11.stem:
Oral histories from residents who lived near a shuttered steel mill describe both pride in steady mid-century wages and lasting resentment over unremediated contamination. A recent soil study confirms elevated heavy metals in yards closest to the old furnaces, with levels declining with distance from the site.

The information most strongly supports which conclusion?

choices.A: All former mill workers want the mill rebuilt exactly as it was.
choices.B: Community memory of economic benefit coexists with evidence and recollection of environmental harm concentrated near the former mill.
choices.C: Heavy metals in the soil came from household paint, not the mill.
choices.D: Resentment has entirely replaced pride in the community's narratives.

rw-inf-11.explanation: Oral histories hold both pride and resentment; soil data show contamination near furnaces—B integrates both. A invents rebuilding desire. C contradicts the distance pattern tied to the mill. D erases the pride strand the text includes.
rw-inf-11.method: Preserve both halves of mixed testimony when the text gives both.
rw-inf-11.speedTip: Distance-declining pollution supports a point-source near the mill, not household paint.
rw-inf-11.commonTrap: Flattening ambivalent community memory into a single emotion or goal.
rw-inf-11.trap: Flattening ambivalent community memory into a single emotion or goal.

rw-inf-12.stem:
When a university moved introductory psychology to a flipped format—video lectures at home, problem-solving in class—exam averages rose by four points, but course withdrawal rates also rose slightly, especially among first-year students who reported limited high-speed internet access.

Which choice is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Flipped classrooms help every student equally.
choices.B: The format shift coincided with higher average exam scores and a small increase in withdrawals that may have been concentrated among students with weaker internet access.
choices.D: Video lectures should replace all in-person teaching.

rw-inf-12.explanation: B reflects the score gain and the withdrawal pattern tied to internet reports. A contradicts unequal withdrawal impacts. C and D contradict or overextend the positive exam result.
rw-inf-12.method: Hold both outcomes (scores up, withdrawals up for a subgroup) in one inference.
rw-inf-12.speedTip: "Every student equally" fails when a subgroup is flagged.
rw-inf-12.commonTrap: Ignoring the equity/internet wrinkle and treating average gains as universal success.
rw-inf-12.trap: Ignoring the equity/internet wrinkle and treating average gains as universal success.

rw-inf-13.stem:
Fossil pollen from a lake core shows a sudden rise in grass pollen and a drop in tree pollen around 3,000 years ago, coinciding with charcoal layers indicating more frequent fires. Human stone tools appear in shoreline sediments in the same interval.

What is the best-supported inference?

choices.A: A shift toward more open, fire-influenced vegetation occurred around 3,000 years ago in this locality, around the time humans were present on the shoreline.
choices.B: Humans were the sole cause of every vegetation change on Earth after 3,000 years ago.
choices.C: Trees went extinct globally 3,000 years ago.
choices.D: Charcoal layers form only when lightning strikes occur.

rw-inf-13.explanation: A stays local and correlative: grasses up, trees down, more fire evidence, humans present. B and C globalize wildly. D invents an exclusive lightning rule.
rw-inf-13.method: Prefer local, time-bounded, correlative wording for paleoecological co-occurrence.
rw-inf-13.speedTip: Global extinction language is almost always a trap here.
rw-inf-13.commonTrap: Scaling a lake-core pattern into a global extinction or sole-cause human claim.
rw-inf-13.trap: Scaling a lake-core pattern into a global extinction or sole-cause human claim.

rw-inf-14.stem:
A nonprofit trained community health workers to visit new parents weekly for three months. Compared with families on a waitlist, visited families had higher rates of completed infant vaccinations at six months. The program was offered only in two zip codes with existing transit access to clinics.

Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.A: Home visits caused higher vaccination completion in the studied zip codes relative to waitlisted families, though the design does not show what would happen in areas without clinic transit access.
choices.B: Vaccinations are unnecessary if home visits occur.
choices.C: The program will work identically in rural areas without clinics.
choices.D: Waitlisted families refused all medical care.

rw-inf-14.explanation: A correctly limits the inference to the studied comparison and notes the transit-access boundary. B and D invent refusal/unnecessary care. C overextends to untested settings.
rw-inf-14.method: Note who was studied and what boundary conditions were stated.
rw-inf-14.speedTip: Waitlist comparison supports efficacy in-sample; geography limits out-of-sample claims.
rw-inf-14.commonTrap: Exporting results to settings the study explicitly didn't include.
rw-inf-14.trap: Exporting results to settings the study explicitly didn't include.

rw-inf-15.stem:
In the novel fragment discovered in a publisher's archive, the protagonist repeatedly postpones mailing a letter confessing a betrayal; each delay is followed by a scene in which a minor character acts with unexpected generosity. The fragment ends before the letter is sent.

Based on the fragment as described, which inference about the text's emerging pattern is best supported?

choices.A: The narrative juxtaposes the protagonist's withheld confession with displays of others' generosity, leaving the confession unresolved in the surviving fragment.
choices.B: The protagonist has already mailed the letter before the fragment begins.
choices.D: The publisher destroyed the novel's ending because it was immoral.

rw-inf-15.explanation: A matches the repeated postpone–generosity pattern and unresolved ending. B contradicts postponement. C contradicts generosity. D invents publisher motives.
rw-inf-15.method: Describe the pattern the stem actually gives; don't invent archival melodrama.
rw-inf-15.speedTip: If the letter isn't sent by the end, answers that say it was sent are wrong.
rw-inf-15.commonTrap: Inventing publication history instead of reading the described narrative pattern.
rw-inf-15.trap: Inventing publication history instead of reading the described narrative pattern.

rw-inf-16.stem:
City open-data logs show that 311 complaints about illegal dumping spiked in precincts where bulk-trash pickup was reduced from weekly to monthly. Precincts that kept weekly pickup showed no similar spike. Demographic profiles of the two precinct groups were similar.

The logs most strongly suggest that

choices.A: residents in reduced-pickup precincts became generally more likely to file all types of complaints.
choices.B: a reduction in bulk-trash pickup frequency was associated with more illegal-dumping complaints where that reduction occurred, compared with similar precincts that retained weekly pickup.
choices.C: illegal dumping is unrelated to municipal services.
choices.D: monthly pickup is preferred by most residents.

rw-inf-16.explanation: The contrast between reduced-pickup precincts (spike) and weekly-pickup precincts (no spike), with similar demographics, supports B. A invents a general complaint tendency. C contradicts the association. D invents preferences.
rw-inf-16.method: Use the differential change across otherwise similar precinct groups.
rw-inf-16.speedTip: Don't upgrade "dumping complaints" into "all complaint types."
rw-inf-16.commonTrap: Broadening a specific complaint spike into a claim about all 311 behavior.
rw-inf-16.trap: Broadening a specific complaint spike into a claim about all 311 behavior.

rw-inf-17.stem:
Linguists recording a minority language found that speakers under 30 used heritage-language vocabulary for food and kinship but switched to the dominant language for science and government topics. Speakers over 60 used the heritage language across nearly all topics. School instruction in the heritage language had been discontinued 25 years earlier.

Which inference is best supported?

choices.A: The heritage language has already vanished completely.
choices.B: Younger speakers' heritage-language use appears domain-limited compared with older speakers' broader use, consistent with reduced institutional support after schooling in the language ended.
choices.C: Older speakers refuse to discuss science.
choices.D: Food vocabulary is harder to learn than scientific vocabulary.

rw-inf-17.explanation: B captures age-based domain differences and links them to the discontinued schooling timeline without claiming total disappearance. A is false given ongoing use. C invents refusal. D invents difficulty rankings.
rw-inf-17.method: Domain restriction ≠ extinction; connect to the schooling detail carefully.
rw-inf-17.speedTip: "Vanished completely" fails if any age group still speaks it.
rw-inf-17.commonTrap: Equating narrowed domains among youth with total language death.
rw-inf-17.trap: Equating narrowed domains among youth with total language death.

rw-inf-18.stem:
An art conservator notes that a fifteenth-century panel painting shows unusually bright blues in areas later shown by spectroscopy to contain a rare, expensive pigment. Adjacent workshop paintings from the same decade use cheaper substitutes in similar iconographic positions.

What is most strongly supported?

choices.A: The panel's patron or workshop allocated comparatively costly materials to this work, at least for the blue passages.
choices.B: All fifteenth-century painters preferred cheap pigments.
choices.D: The panel is a nineteenth-century forgery.

rw-inf-18.explanation: Costly pigment here vs. cheaper substitutes next door supports a relatively higher material investment in this panel's blues. B contradicts this panel's evidence. C and D are unsupported.
rw-inf-18.method: Comparative material cost → inference about allocation/investment, not authenticity panic.
rw-inf-18.speedTip: Rare pigment presence argues against casual forgery claims without more evidence.
rw-inf-18.commonTrap: Jumping to forgery when the data are about pigment expense and workshop comparison.
rw-inf-18.trap: Jumping to forgery when the data are about pigment expense and workshop comparison.

rw-inf-19.stem:
After a hospital introduced a checklist for central-line insertions, bloodstream infection rates fell by half within a year. During the same year, the hospital also hired more infection-control nurses and remodeled two intensive-care units. A neighboring hospital that adopted only the checklist (without extra nurses or remodeling) saw a smaller but still meaningful infection drop.

Which choice is best supported?

choices.A: Remodeling alone caused the entire decline at the first hospital.
choices.B: The checklist likely contributed to infection reduction, since a hospital that implemented the checklist without the other changes also saw a meaningful drop, though additional measures may have amplified effects at the first hospital.

rw-inf-19.explanation: The neighbor's checklist-only improvement supports checklist contribution; the larger drop where multiple changes occurred allows that other measures may amplify—B. A ignores the neighbor evidence. C and D contradict parts of the results.
rw-inf-19.method: Use the second hospital as a natural comparison to isolate checklist contribution.
rw-inf-19.speedTip: Multi-change settings need careful language: "contributed" not "sole cause."
rw-inf-19.commonTrap: Attributing the entire effect to remodeling despite checklist-only gains elsewhere.
rw-inf-19.trap: Attributing the entire effect to remodeling despite checklist-only gains elsewhere.

rw-inf-20.stem:
A sports economist finds that when a mid-size city hosts a short amateur championship, hotel occupancy jumps during the event week, but annual museum attendance and downtown retail employment show no lasting change in the following year compared with similar cities that did not host.

The findings most strongly support the conclusion that

choices.A: amateur championships permanently transform host-city economies.
choices.B: the event is associated with a temporary hospitality boost rather than durable gains in museum attendance or retail employment, relative to non-host peer cities.
choices.D: hotel workers leave the city after every event.

rw-inf-20.explanation: Occupancy jump plus no lasting museum/retail change vs. peers supports a temporary hospitality effect—B. A contradicts "no lasting change." C and D invent closures and out-migration.
rw-inf-20.method: Separate short-run hospitality spike from long-run cultural/retail null results.
rw-inf-20.speedTip: "Permanently transform" is incompatible with null annual follow-up findings.
rw-inf-20.commonTrap: Treating a one-week hotel spike as proof of lasting economic transformation.
rw-inf-20.trap: Treating a one-week hotel spike as proof of lasting economic transformation.

rw-m2-01.stem:
The archive preserves correspondence between the two composers ______ letters reveal a decade-long argument about whether folk melodies should be quoted verbatim or thoroughly transformed.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rw-m2-01.explanation: Both clauses are independent, so a semicolon is appropriate. A comma alone creates a splice; no punctuation creates a run-on; the colon plus comma after 'these' is ungrammatical.
rw-m2-01.method: If both sides can stand alone, join with a semicolon, period, or comma+FANBOYS—not a bare comma.
rw-m2-01.speedTip: Long academic clauses still splice if joined by a comma only.
rw-m2-01.commonTrap: Comma splice hidden by a lengthy second clause.

rw-m2-02.stem:
The biographer refuses to ______ her subject's contradictions: she presents the reformer's generosity and her ruthlessness as mutually illuminating rather than as errors to be smoothed away.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rw-m2-02.explanation: Refusing to smooth contradictions away means refusing to cut them out—excise. Cataloging would be listing them (which she does); amplify and translate do not match 'smoothed away.'
rw-m2-02.method: Let the colon define the blank; match 'not smoothed away.'
rw-m2-02.speedTip: Colon after a blank often equals a free definition.
rw-m2-02.commonTrap: 'Catalog' because biographies list traits—yet she is not refusing to list them.

rw-m2-03.stem:
Early reviews dismissed the sculpture as unfinished because its surfaces were deliberately rough. ______ later critics treated that roughness as the work's central argument against polished monumentality.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rw-m2-03.explanation: The hinge is temporal (early → later revaluation). 'In due course' fits. Same token/accordingly imply agreement or result; for instance introduces an example.
rw-m2-03.method: Prefer time transitions when the sentences are ordered by historical reception.
rw-m2-03.speedTip: Early/later markers beat logic transitions when chronology is the link.
rw-m2-03.commonTrap: 'Accordingly,' as if dismissal caused the later praise.

rw-m2-04.stem:
Believing the old maps unreliable, ______ anew using satellite imagery and oral histories from coastal villages.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the cartography team charted the shoreline's contours
choices.B: the shoreline's contours were charted by the cartography team
choices.C: charting the shoreline's contours was undertaken by the cartography team
choices.D: the shoreline's contours, charted by the cartography team,

rw-m2-04.explanation: 'Believing…' must modify the believers—the cartography team. Only the choice that places the team as subject is correct; options that make the shoreline's contours the subject (including passive and fragment forms) dangle.
rw-m2-04.method: Match the participial opener to the grammatical subject that follows.
rw-m2-04.speedTip: Passive subjects after -ing openers usually signal danglers.
rw-m2-04.commonTrap: Letting 'shoreline's contours' follow so inanimate contours seem to 'believe.'

rw-m2-05.stem:
Text 1
A longitudinal study of bilingual schoolchildren found that those who received literacy instruction in both languages outperformed monolingually instructed peers on metalinguistic awareness tasks by grade 4.

Text 2
Psychologist Omar Reed cautions that many bilingual programs also provide smaller class sizes and more specialized teachers. Without isolating those resources, he argues, researchers cannot attribute gains solely to dual-language instruction.

Based on the texts, what would Reed (Text 2) most likely say about the study in Text 1?

choices.A: It proves that metalinguistic awareness cannot improve after grade 4.
choices.B: Its conclusion may overstate the unique effect of bilingual instruction if other program resources differed.
choices.C: It should have measured only monolingual students.
choices.D: It demonstrates that class size is irrelevant to literacy outcomes.

rw-m2-05.explanation: Reed worries about confounders (class size, specialized teachers). He would question whether Text 1 isolated bilingual instruction. A, C, and D invent positions he does not take.
rw-m2-05.method: Project Text 2's caveat onto Text 1's causal claim.
rw-m2-05.speedTip: Confounder critiques → answers about overstated unique effects.

rw-m2-06.stem:
The following text is from a 1924 review of a travel memoir.

The author collects impressions the way some travelers collect luggage labels—eagerly, indiscriminately, and with little interest in whether any two belong on the same journey. What the book gains in abundance it forfeits in design.

Which choice best describes the function of the phrase "the way some travelers collect luggage labels" in the text as a whole?

choices.C: It supplies a simile that clarifies the author's indiscriminate method of gathering material.
choices.A: It identifies the memoir's primary audience as frequent travelers.
choices.B: It praises the author's careful organization of chapters.
choices.D: It introduces statistical evidence about tourism.

rw-m2-06.explanation: The simile explains indiscriminate collecting and sets up the abundance-vs-design critique. It does not name audience, praise organization, or give statistics.
rw-m2-06.method: Ask what argumentative work the comparison does.
rw-m2-06.speedTip: Figurative phrases usually clarify a praise or blame already underway.
rw-m2-06.commonTrap: Literal reading that the book targets travelers with luggage labels.

rw-m2-07.stem:
Several of the recovered manuscripts were written in a cipher ______ only recently deciphered using frequency analysis and a partial key found in a merchant's ledger.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rw-m2-07.explanation: A restrictive relative clause needs 'that was.' A is a splice; B is a run-on; a semicolon cannot introduce a dependent which-clause.
rw-m2-07.method: If the continuation cannot stand alone, use a relative clause—not ; or a new independent clause.
rw-m2-07.speedTip: Semicolon + which/that is almost always wrong.
rw-m2-07.commonTrap: Comma splice with 'it was' after a dense noun phrase.

rw-m2-08.stem:
When a city capped ride-hail vehicles in the downtown core, average evening wait times rose from 3 minutes to 11 minutes, while late-night transit ridership on parallel bus routes increased 14%. Daytime wait times and daytime bus ridership barely changed.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the cap appears to have shifted some evening travel toward buses without similarly affecting daytime patterns.
choices.B: riders abandoned buses entirely once wait times increased.
choices.C: the cap reduced transit ridership across all hours of the day.
choices.D: wait times are the only factor travelers consider when choosing a mode.

rw-m2-08.explanation: Evening waits and evening bus use both rose; daytime metrics were flat—so any shift is evening-specific. B and C contradict the ridership rise; D overclaims.
rw-m2-08.method: Preserve the study's day/evening split in the inference.
rw-m2-08.commonTrap: All-day generalizations that ignore 'daytime barely changed.'

rw-m2-09.stem:
Rather than offering a ______ narrative of the expedition, the journal proceeds by sharp juxtapositions—storm and calm, hunger and sudden plenty—that leave causal links for the reader to supply.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rw-m2-09.explanation: 'Rather than' sets up a contrast with discontinuous juxtapositions, so the missing word is seamless (continuous/smooth). Fragmentary restates the juxtapositions; polemical and anonymous are unrelated.
rw-m2-09.method: Rather than X, Y → X is the antonym of Y's method.
rw-m2-09.speedTip: 'Rather than' = hunt the opposite of what follows.
rw-m2-09.commonTrap: 'Fragmentary,' which agrees with juxtapositions instead of contrasting them.

rw-m2-10.stem:
A student preparing a presentation on urban bee hotels records these notes:
• Study 1 (2019): bee hotels in dense neighborhoods hosted mostly nonnative bees.
• Study 2 (2021): hotels placed beside native wildflower strips hosted a higher share of native bees.
• City parks department installed 40 hotels in 2020 with no accompanying plantings.
• A 2022 follow-up found those park hotels mirrored Study 1's nonnative-heavy pattern.
• Experts recommend pairing hotels with native forage.

The student wants to recommend a design change for the city's bee-hotel program. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.C: Because hotels without plantings hosted mostly nonnative bees—while hotels beside native wildflowers hosted more natives—the city should add native forage beside existing hotels.
choices.A: The parks department installed 40 bee hotels in 2020.
choices.B: Study 1 and the 2022 follow-up both examined bee hotels in urban settings.
choices.D: Experts have written extensively about pollinator decline worldwide.

rw-m2-10.explanation: Only the choice that both uses the planting contrast and states a concrete design recommendation fits the goal. Bare installation counts, study-setting summaries, and off-notes claims about worldwide decline do not recommend a change.
rw-m2-10.method: Match the verb in the goal ('recommend') to a choice that proposes an action.
rw-m2-10.speedTip: If the goal says recommend, eliminate choices that never recommend.
rw-m2-10.commonTrap: Accurate study summaries that never propose a change.

rw-m2-11.stem:
The following text is adapted from a philosopher's preface.

I have not tried to say everything that might be said about habit. Completeness of that sort usually conceals the very pattern it claims to display, as a crowded shelf can hide the shape of the room. My aim is narrower: to make a few stubborn features of habit visible enough to argue about.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.D: To justify limiting the book's scope so that key features of habit remain discussable.
choices.A: To apologize for omitting footnotes from the preface.
choices.B: To argue that habit cannot be studied philosophically.
choices.C: To summarize every major theory of habit in chronological order.

rw-m2-11.explanation: The author rejects total completeness as obscuring and states a narrower aim—making stubborn features visible for argument. That justifies limited scope. B invents footnotes; C and D contradict the stated aim.
rw-m2-11.method: Prefaces often justify method/scope; match that speech act.
rw-m2-11.speedTip: When authors say what they will not do, purpose is often delimiting scope.
rw-m2-11.commonTrap: Reading the crowded-shelf image as 'habit is unknowable.'

rw-m2-12.stem:
The director requested that the lighting designer ______ the intensity of the blue wash before Saturday's preview.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rw-m2-12.explanation: After request/demand/insist + that, formal English uses the base subjunctive: reduce (not reduces).
rw-m2-12.method: Mandate verbs + that → base form of the next verb.
rw-m2-12.speedTip: Subjunctive: drop the -s even with singular subjects.

rw-m2-13.stem:
The treaty required factories to install scrubbers by 2010. ______ emissions inventories show that several signatories missed the deadline by more than five years yet still claimed full compliance in public reports.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rw-m2-13.explanation: A strict requirement is followed by missed deadlines and false compliance claims—contrast. Nevertheless fits. The other options wrongly imply alignment, similarity, or purposeful follow-through.
rw-m2-13.speedTip: Eliminate transitions that assume success when the second sentence reports failure.
rw-m2-13.commonTrap: 'To that end,' as if the inventories illustrate successful implementation.

rw-m2-14.stem:
Geographer Lena Okoye argues that informal street markets survive not despite municipal regulation but because certain regulations—such as limited vending licenses—create scarcity that raises the value of established stalls.

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okoye's argument?

choices.C: In cities that abolished vending licenses, informal markets remained as stable as before, and stall sale prices did not fall.
choices.A: Some street markets celebrate annual festivals that attract tourists.
choices.B: Vendors often borrow money from relatives to stock their stalls.
choices.D: Municipal inspectors sometimes overlook minor permit violations.

rw-m2-14.explanation: Okoye's mechanism is license-driven scarcity raising stall value. If abolishing licenses leaves stability and prices unchanged, scarcity from licenses is not doing the explanatory work. B–D are irrelevant to that mechanism.
rw-m2-14.method: Weaken a because-claim by removing the predicted effect when the cause is removed.
rw-m2-14.speedTip: Causal weakeners flip the expected correlation.
rw-m2-14.commonTrap: Colorful vendor details that never test scarcity or prices.

rw-m2-15.stem:
A lab compared two methods for cleaning historic textiles. Method A removed more surface soot in one hour, but fibers showed microscopic fraying. Method B removed less soot in the same time yet left fiber structure intact. Conservators later chose Method B for a fragile tapestry while using Method A only on sturdy upholstery.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.D: conservators appear to weigh material durability alongside cleaning speed when selecting a method.
choices.A: Method A is universally preferred for all historic textiles.
choices.B: soot removal is irrelevant to conservation decisions.
choices.C: Method B works more quickly than Method A on every fabric.

rw-m2-15.explanation: The split use—B for fragile, A for sturdy—implies durability is weighed with cleaning power/speed. B and D contradict the choices made; C contradicts concern with soot and fibers.
rw-m2-15.method: Infer the decision rule implied by divergent applications.
rw-m2-15.speedTip: Different treatments for different objects → a conditional rule.
rw-m2-15.commonTrap: Universal preference claims that erase the sturdy/fragile split.

rw-m2-16.stem:
The following text is from an essay on scientific diagrams.

A diagram that merely decorates a page may please the eye while teaching nothing. By contrast, a diagram that forces the reader to trace a relationship—input to output, cause to effect—turns looking into a form of reasoning.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It contrasts two kinds of diagrams and elevates the kind that engages reasoning.
choices.B: It recounts the history of diagram-making from antiquity to the present.
choices.C: It lists laboratory tools required to print scientific figures.
choices.D: It argues that all illustrations should be removed from scientific papers.

rw-m2-16.explanation: Sentence 1 critiques decorative diagrams; sentence 2 elevates relationship-tracing diagrams. That is a contrast-and-preference structure. B–D invent history, tools, or a ban.
rw-m2-16.method: Label each sentence's move (critique / contrast / preference).
rw-m2-16.speedTip: 'By contrast' nearly announces a contrast structure.
rw-m2-16.commonTrap: Overreading the critique as a call to ban all illustrations.

rw-m2-17.stem:
The curator insisted on one nonnegotiable condition ______ every loaned painting had to arrive with a condition report signed within the previous thirty days.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rw-m2-17.explanation: Two independent clauses: semicolon works. A splices; C runs on; D needs a comma before 'and' if used as a coordinator and still reads awkwardly without restating the relationship.
rw-m2-17.speedTip: A colon could also introduce an elaboration, but among these options the semicolon is cleanest and correct.

rw-m2-18.stem:
Economist Marisol Vega claims that publishing restaurant health-inspection scores in a simple letter grade (A–C) changes consumer behavior more than publishing the same data as raw point totals.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vega's claim?

choices.C: In a controlled roll-out, neighborhoods that received letter grades showed larger shifts toward higher-scoring restaurants than neighborhoods that received only point totals.
choices.A: Some restaurants voluntarily display certificates in their windows.
choices.B: Health inspectors visit restaurants at unannounced times.
choices.D: Raw point totals can be converted into letter grades with a fixed formula.

rw-m2-18.explanation: Support requires a comparative behavioral effect of letter grades vs. point totals. A provides that comparison. B–D never measure consumer shifts.
rw-m2-18.method: Rewrite the claim as A changes behavior more than B; demand that comparison.
rw-m2-18.commonTrap: True background facts about inspections that skip consumer behavior.

rw-m2-19.stem:
Anyone who submits a portfolio before May 1 will receive ______ results by email within two weeks.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rw-m2-19.explanation: Singular 'Anyone' commonly takes the gender-neutral singular 'their' in current Standard English conventions tested on the Digital SAT; 'its' wrongly treats a person as an object; contractions are wrong here.
rw-m2-19.method: Need a possessive pronoun for a person of unspecified gender; their is accepted.
rw-m2-19.commonTrap: 'Its' agreeing in number but not in animacy/personhood.

rw-m2-20.stem:
While drafting a report on heat-resilient housing, a student takes these notes:
• Reflective 'cool roofs' can lower indoor temperatures by 2–5°C in tests.
• Exterior shade screens reduced cooling-energy use 12% in a 2020 trial.
• Insulation upgrades cut heat gain but showed smaller short-term temperature drops than cool roofs.
• Upfront cost: cool roofs (moderate), screens (low), insulation (high).
• The student's audience is a city council seeking the fastest indoor-temperature relief per dollar.

The student wants to recommend the option that best matches the council's priority. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Because the council wants fast indoor-temperature relief per dollar, cool roofs—moderate cost with 2–5°C tested drops—outperform pricier insulation's smaller short-term drops; shade screens also help energy use but are framed mainly around energy, not temperature.
choices.B: Insulation upgrades reduce heat gain but cost more upfront than cool roofs.
choices.C: Shade screens reduced cooling-energy use by 12% in 2020.
choices.D: Cool roofs, shade screens, and insulation upgrades have all been studied in recent trials.

rw-m2-20.explanation: The priority is fastest temperature relief per dollar. B ties cool roofs' temperature drops and moderate cost to that priority and contrasts insulation. the other options give partial facts; D is a vague overview.
rw-m2-20.method: Audience priority in the notes is the scoring rubric for the recommendation.
rw-m2-20.speedTip: Circle the audience goal before reading choices.
rw-m2-20.commonTrap: Energy-use statistics when the stated priority is temperature per dollar.

rw-m2-21.stem:
The senator's apology was widely criticized as ______: it acknowledged harm in abstract terms while carefully avoiding any admission that specific decisions had been wrong.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rw-m2-21.explanation: Abstract acknowledgment without admitting specific wrongs describes a shallow, box-checking apology—perfunctory. Unequivocal is the opposite; magnanimous and spontaneous do not fit the careful evasion.
rw-m2-21.method: Match the blank to the behavior after the colon.
rw-m2-21.commonTrap: 'Unequivocal,' a hard word that reverses the meaning.

rw-m2-22.stem:
In a randomized classroom study, students who wrote weekly one-sentence summaries of each lecture scored higher on delayed exams than students who reread highlights for the same total time. On immediate quizzes given the same day, the two groups scored nearly identically.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.C: summary writing may aid longer-term retention more than it boosts same-day performance relative to rereading.
choices.A: rereading highlights is superior for long-term retention.
choices.B: immediate quizzes are harder than delayed exams.
choices.D: one-sentence summaries take more total time than rereading.

rw-m2-22.explanation: Same-day parity plus delayed advantage for summarizers supports a long-term-specific benefit. B reverses the delayed result; the other options are unsupported.
rw-m2-22.method: Use both time horizons; the inference should explain the divergence.
rw-m2-22.speedTip: Same now, different later → retention/delay effect.
rw-m2-22.commonTrap: Claiming overall superiority without the delayed/immediate split.

rw-m2-23.stem:
Text 1
A meta-analysis of remote-work studies reports that employees with fully flexible schedules report higher job satisfaction but slightly lower rates of promotion over five years.

Text 2
Sociologist Keisha Brandt argues that promotion gaps in remote cohorts often reflect evaluation systems designed around visible office presence rather than weaker remote performance itself.

Based on the texts, how would Brandt (Text 2) most likely interpret the promotion finding in Text 1?

choices.D: As a pattern that may stem from presence-biased evaluation, not from flexible work reducing capability.
choices.A: As evidence that flexible schedules make employees less competent.
choices.B: As proof that job satisfaction and promotion rates always move together.
choices.C: As a reason to eliminate all remote-work options immediately.

rw-m2-23.explanation: Brandt attributes gaps to presence-biased evaluation systems, so she would reinterpret Text 1's promotion finding that way. the other choices misrepresent her view.
rw-m2-23.method: Answer in Brandt's vocabulary: evaluation design vs. performance.
rw-m2-23.speedTip: Text 2 authors often reframe Text 1 causes without denying Text 1 facts.

rw-m2-24.stem:
The first experiment measured only outdoor particulate levels near the factory. ______ the second experiment placed sensors inside nearby homes to test whether outdoor spikes translated into indoor exposure.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rw-m2-24.explanation: Experiment 2 extends experiment 1's limited outdoor-only scope indoors. 'Building on that limited scope' captures expansion. In other words restates; otherwise contrasts alternatives; similarly claims sameness rather than extension.
rw-m2-24.method: Identify whether sentence 2 restates, contrasts, or extends sentence 1.
rw-m2-24.speedTip: Second experiment that adds a measurement = extension/building-on.

rw-m2-25.stem:
The following text is adapted from a 1930s nature column.

Call the weed a villain if the garden's goal is parade-ground uniformity. Call it a tutor if the goal is to learn which soils flood, which bake, and which quietly support more life than the manicured rows admit.

Which choice best describes the function of the two sentences together in the text?

choices.B: They show that the same plant can be judged differently depending on the gardener's purpose.
choices.A: They provide a step-by-step method for eradicating weeds.
choices.C: They claim that uniformity is the only legitimate garden goal.
choices.D: They present rainfall data for two soil types.

rw-m2-25.explanation: Parallel 'Call it…' frames reverse the weed's status based on goals—villain vs. tutor—so judgment depends on purpose. B–D contradict or invent content.
rw-m2-25.method: Parallel imperatives with opposite labels → purpose-relative evaluation.
rw-m2-25.speedTip: Mirrored sentence openings often signal a contrast the author wants you to notice.
rw-m2-25.commonTrap: Assuming the author endorses uniformity because it appears first.

rw-m2-26.stem:
A student is writing a caption for a museum exhibit on early radio and takes these notes:
• 1920: KDKA broadcasts U.S. election returns—often cited as a commercial radio milestone.
• 1910s: hobbyists already shared music and news on amateur sets.
• Historian Ruiz: commercial milestones get remembered; amateur networks made the audience.
• The exhibit's theme is 'who created the listening public?'
• A 1922 magazine estimated one million amateur operators worldwide.

The student wants the caption to challenge the idea that commercial stations alone created the listening public. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.C: Although KDKA's 1920 broadcast is remembered as a milestone, amateur networks in the 1910s—and an estimated one million operators by 1922—had already cultivated listeners, as Ruiz argues.
choices.A: KDKA's 1920 election broadcast is frequently cited as a commercial radio milestone.
choices.B: A 1922 magazine estimated one million amateur operators worldwide.
choices.D: The exhibit asks who created the listening public.

rw-m2-26.explanation: Challenging commercial-alone creation requires both the commercial milestone and prior amateur networks/audience. B does that with Ruiz. A reinforces the commercial story; the other options are incomplete.
rw-m2-26.method: Goal = challenge X → include X and the counter-evidence.
rw-m2-26.speedTip: Challenge captions must name the claim they push against.
rw-m2-26.commonTrap: Repeating the famous commercial milestone without the challenge.

rw-m2-27.stem:
Shipments of a rare medicinal bark fell after source countries expanded protected forest zones. Pharmaceutical intermediaries reported stable retail prices, however, because they drew down stockpiled bark purchased in earlier years. When those stockpiles neared depletion, retail prices rose sharply within one quarter.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.D: stockpiles temporarily masked the price effects of reduced shipments until reserves ran low.
choices.A: protected forests had no effect on bark availability.
choices.B: retail prices are fixed by law and cannot change.
choices.C: intermediaries increased shipments as soon as protections expanded.

rw-m2-27.explanation: Stable prices during drawdown plus a sharp rise at depletion imply stockpiles delayed the price signal. the other choices contradict the passage.
rw-m2-27.method: Connect the delayed price jump to the stockpile mechanism stated mid-passage.
rw-m2-27.speedTip: When prices stay flat then jump, look for a buffer that emptied.
rw-m2-27.commonTrap: Claiming protections did nothing because prices were briefly stable.

rw-synth-01.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Hoover Dam was completed in 1936 on the Colorado River.
• It generates hydroelectric power for parts of Nevada, Arizona, and California.
• Lake Mead, the reservoir created by the dam, has faced historically low water levels in recent drought years.
• The dam is a major tourist attraction, drawing about 7 million visitors in peak years.

The student wants to emphasize a contemporary environmental challenge related to the dam. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Completed in 1936, the Hoover Dam generates hydroelectric power for Nevada, Arizona, and California.
choices.B: Lake Mead, the reservoir created by the Hoover Dam, has faced historically low water levels in recent drought years.
choices.C: The Hoover Dam draws about 7 million visitors in peak years as a major tourist attraction.
choices.D: The Hoover Dam was completed in 1936 on the Colorado River and remains a tourist attraction.

rw-synth-01.explanation: The goal is a contemporary environmental challenge: low Lake Mead levels in drought years. B delivers that. A is power generation history, C is tourism, D mixes completion date and tourism—none emphasize the environmental challenge.
rw-synth-01.method: Underline the goal words (contemporary environmental challenge); keep only notes that match.
rw-synth-01.speedTip: Ignore impressive but off-goal facts (tourism numbers, completion year).
rw-synth-01.commonTrap: Choosing famous dam facts instead of the drought/water-level challenge named in the goal.
rw-synth-01.trap: Choosing famous dam facts instead of the drought/water-level challenge named in the goal.

rw-synth-02.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Composer Florence Price (1887–1953) was the first African American woman to have a symphony performed by a major U.S. orchestra.
• Her Symphony No. 1 in E Minor premiered with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra in 1933.
• Many of her manuscripts were rediscovered in an abandoned house in Illinois in 2009.
• Orchestras have programmed her works more frequently since that rediscovery.

The student wants to introduce Price to an audience unfamiliar with her and highlight a landmark "first." Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Many of Florence Price's manuscripts were rediscovered in an abandoned Illinois house in 2009.
choices.B: Orchestras have programmed Florence Price's works more frequently in recent years.
choices.C: Florence Price (1887–1953) was the first African American woman to have a symphony performed by a major U.S. orchestra, when her Symphony No. 1 premiered with the Chicago Symphony in 1933.
choices.D: Florence Price wrote Symphony No. 1 in E Minor.

rw-synth-02.explanation: The goal needs an introduction plus a landmark first. C names her, dates her, states the "first," and cites the 1933 premiere. A and B are about rediscovery/reception, not the landmark first. D is too thin to introduce her properly.
rw-synth-02.method: Match BOTH parts of a compound goal: introduce + landmark first.
rw-synth-02.speedTip: Rediscovery notes are tempting but wrong if the goal is her historic premiere.
rw-synth-02.commonTrap: Answering with the rediscovery story when the goal asks for her pioneering premiere.
rw-synth-02.trap: Answering with the rediscovery story when the goal asks for her pioneering premiere.

rw-synth-03.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool adapted from a bacterial immune system.
• It can cut DNA at targeted locations guided by a short RNA sequence.
• Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR research.
• Ethical debates continue over germline editing in human embryos.

The student wants to explain the basic mechanism of CRISPR-Cas9 without discussing prizes or ethics. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR research.
choices.B: Ethical debates continue over germline editing in human embryos using CRISPR-related methods.
choices.C: Adapted from a bacterial immune system, CRISPR-Cas9 uses a short RNA guide to cut DNA at targeted locations.
choices.D: CRISPR-Cas9 is famous because its inventors won a Nobel Prize amid ongoing ethical debates.

rw-synth-03.explanation: The goal is mechanism only—no prizes or ethics. C explains bacterial origin, RNA guide, and targeted cutting. A is prizes, B is ethics, D mixes both excluded topics.
rw-synth-03.method: When the goal says "without X," delete any choice that includes X.
rw-synth-03.speedTip: Scan choices for banned topics first; eliminate fast.
rw-synth-03.commonTrap: Including Nobel/ethics content because those notes feel important, despite the "without" clause.
rw-synth-03.trap: Including Nobel/ethics content because those notes feel important, despite the "without" clause.

rw-synth-04.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Inca road system (Qhapaq Ñan) stretched thousands of kilometers across western South America.
• Roads linked the capital Cusco to provincial centers.
• Rope suspension bridges helped span deep Andean valleys.
• Spanish colonial accounts describe chasquis (relay runners) carrying messages along the roads.

The student wants to emphasize how the road system overcame difficult mountain terrain. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Spanish colonial accounts describe chasquis carrying messages along Inca roads.
choices.B: The Inca road system linked Cusco to provincial centers across western South America.
choices.C: Rope suspension bridges on the Inca road system helped span deep Andean valleys.
choices.D: The Qhapaq Ñan stretched thousands of kilometers.

rw-synth-04.explanation: Overcoming mountain terrain is best captured by rope bridges spanning Andean valleys. A is messengers, B is political linkage, D is length alone—none focus on terrain challenges.
rw-synth-04.method: Goal keyword = mountain terrain → bridges/valleys beat length or messengers.
rw-synth-04.speedTip: Length ≠ terrain difficulty; look for valleys/bridges.
rw-synth-04.commonTrap: Picking scale (thousands of km) instead of the terrain-engineering detail.
rw-synth-04.trap: Picking scale (thousands of km) instead of the terrain-engineering detail.

rw-synth-05.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Urban beekeeping has grown in several North American cities since 2010.
• A Toronto study found that city honeybee colonies can have strong honey yields.
• Ecologists warn that dense urban hive placement may increase competition with wild native bees for floral resources.
• Some cities now require minimum distances between new hives.

The student wants to present a contrast between a potential benefit of urban beekeeping and an ecological concern. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Urban beekeeping has grown in several North American cities since 2010.
choices.B: Some cities now require minimum distances between new hives.
choices.C: Although a Toronto study found that city honeybee colonies can have strong honey yields, ecologists warn that dense urban hives may increase competition with wild native bees for floral resources.
choices.D: Ecologists study both honeybees and wild native bees in cities.

rw-synth-05.explanation: The goal needs benefit + concern in contrast. C pairs strong yields with competition warnings using "Although." A is growth trend only, B is policy only, D is vague and unused.
rw-synth-05.method: Contrast goals need both sides in one sentence, usually with a contrast word.
rw-synth-05.speedTip: Policy notes aren't the contrast unless the goal asks for regulation.
rw-synth-05.commonTrap: Giving only growth or only a rule when the goal asks for benefit-versus-concern.
rw-synth-05.trap: Giving only growth or only a rule when the goal asks for benefit-versus-concern.

rw-synth-06.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mary Anning (1799–1847) collected fossils along England's Jurassic Coast.
• She discovered the first complete Ichthyosaurus skeleton recognized by science when she was still a teenager.
• Anning's findings informed early vertebrate paleontology.
• During her lifetime, women were rarely admitted to learned scientific societies.
