choices.A: The textiles have already been permanently damaged.
choices.B: Short-term dehumidification alone is unlikely to keep humidity stably within the safe range under current HVAC cycling.
choices.C: The museum should cancel all future textile exhibits.
choices.D: Humidity sensors are generally unreliable in museums.

hp-rw-es-09.explanation: Evidence shows temporary fixes and overnight rebounds tied to HVAC off-cycles → inference that short-term dehumidifiers won't hold steady. A/C/D overreach.
hp-rw-es-09.method: Stay inside the text: temporary fix + rebound = stability problem.
hp-rw-es-09.speedTip: Reject extremes (already ruined / cancel forever / sensors always bad).
hp-rw-es-09.commonTrap: Catastrophic or universal claims beyond the gallery facts.

hp-rw-es-10.stem:
City planners note that bus ridership on Route 12 rose after frequency increased from every 30 minutes to every 12 minutes, even though fares stayed the same and the route map was unchanged.

Which inference is best supported?

choices.C: For Route 12, more frequent service was associated with higher ridership without a fare cut or route redesign.
choices.A: Fare price is irrelevant to ridership on every city route.
choices.B: Riders switched from Route 12 to rideshare services.
choices.D: The city will eventually make all buses free.

hp-rw-es-10.explanation: B restates the observed association tightly. A universalizes; C contradicts the rise; D invents policy.
hp-rw-es-10.method: Prefer the narrow restatement over sweeping policy claims.
hp-rw-es-10.speedTip: Same fare + same map + higher frequency + higher ridership → say exactly that.
hp-rw-es-10.commonTrap: Generalizing one route to all routes or inventing future free transit.

hp-rw-es-11.stem:
Lab notebooks show that Trial 3 of an enzyme experiment was discarded because the water bath overheated by 8°C for twenty minutes. Trials 1, 2, and 4, run at the target temperature, produced tightly clustered reaction rates.

What is most strongly supported?

choices.A: The researchers treated the overheated run as noncomparable to the on-target trials.
choices.B: Temperature control problems make all enzyme experiments worthless.
choices.C: Trial 3's rate would have matched the others if measured carefully.
choices.D: Enzymes never function above the target temperature.

hp-rw-es-11.explanation: Discarding Trial 3 for overheating implies they saw it as noncomparable. A/D are absolute; C invents a counterfactual rate.
hp-rw-es-11.method: Ask what the discard decision itself reveals.
hp-rw-es-11.speedTip: Discarded for heat spike → noncomparable; don't invent numbers.
hp-rw-es-11.commonTrap: Absolute claims about all enzymes or all experiments.

hp-rw-es-12.stem:
A review of apartment listings finds that units advertising in-unit laundry rent for more than similar-sized units in the same buildings without that amenity, after adjusting for floor level and natural light.

Which inference is most reasonable?

choices.D: Within these buildings, in-unit laundry is associated with a rent premium beyond floor and light differences.
choices.A: In-unit laundry is the only amenity tenants value.
choices.C: Tenants dislike shared laundry rooms for health reasons.

hp-rw-es-12.explanation: Adjusted comparison supports an association/premium for laundry. A 'only', C illegality, and D motives go beyond data.
hp-rw-es-12.method: Association after controls is not sole cause or illegal motive.
hp-rw-es-12.speedTip: Say associated with higher rent—stop there.

hp-rw-es-13.stem:
When a library moved popular graphic novels from a back corner to freestanding shelves near the entrance, checkout rates for that collection rose within two weeks while staffing and total open hours stayed constant.

Which inference is best supported?

choices.A: Placement nearer the entrance likely contributed to increased graphic-novel checkouts under otherwise stable operations.
choices.B: Graphic novels are more educational than novels.
choices.C: The library reduced spending on other books.
choices.D: Entrance shelves always increase checkouts for every genre.

hp-rw-es-13.explanation: Timing + stable staffing/hours + location change supports placement as a likely contributor. B/C unsupported; D overgeneralizes.
hp-rw-es-13.method: Change one variable, hold others → cautious inference.
hp-rw-es-13.commonTrap: Universal shelf rules or unrelated collection budgets.

hp-rw-es-14.stem:
A seed company reports that Variety R germinated at 92% in cool soil trays and 61% in warm soil trays under otherwise identical watering and light.

What can most reasonably be concluded?

choices.C: Under these tray conditions, cooler soil was associated with higher germination for Variety R than warmer soil.
choices.A: Variety R will fail outdoors in every warm climate.
choices.B: Watering is more important than temperature for all seeds.
choices.D: Variety R needs darkness to germinate.

hp-rw-es-14.explanation: B mirrors the controlled comparison. A universalizes outdoors; C invents watering primacy; D invents darkness.
hp-rw-es-14.method: Report the association the experiment actually shows.
hp-rw-es-14.speedTip: Cool > warm germination here—don't invent field failure.
hp-rw-es-14.commonTrap: Absolute climate predictions from tray data.

hp-rw-es-15.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile is designed for a multi-year wide-field sky survey.
• Its camera will repeatedly image large stretches of sky to detect changing or moving objects.
• Science goals include mapping dark matter structure and spotting near-Earth asteroids.
• First light engineering tests began in the mid-2020s.

The student wants to emphasize the observatory's dual science goals. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile began engineering tests in the mid-2020s.
choices.B: Designed for a multi-year wide-field survey, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory aims both to map dark matter structure and to spot near-Earth asteroids by repeatedly imaging large sky regions.
choices.C: The observatory's camera will repeatedly image large stretches of sky.
choices.D: Chile hosts the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

hp-rw-es-15.explanation: Dual goals = dark matter + asteroids, with survey method for coherence. B includes both goals. A/D are location/timeline; C is method only.
hp-rw-es-15.method: Goal says dual → need both science aims in one sentence.
hp-rw-es-15.speedTip: If the ask is 'both X and Y,' the correct choice names X and Y.
hp-rw-es-15.commonTrap: Picking timeline or location when the goal is scientific aims.

hp-rw-es-16.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bamboo charcoal can be added to soil to improve water retention in sandy plots.
• A 2022 garden trial found tomato plants in charcoal-amended sand needed fewer waterings.
• Bamboo charcoal is produced by heating bamboo at high temperature in low oxygen.
• Some gardeners dislike charcoal dust because it stains hands and tools.

The student wants to explain how bamboo charcoal is made, without discussing gardening results. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

choices.A: Bamboo charcoal, made by heating bamboo at high temperature in low oxygen, helped tomato plants need fewer waterings in sandy soil.
choices.B: Bamboo charcoal is produced by heating bamboo at high temperature in low oxygen.
choices.C: Gardeners sometimes dislike charcoal dust because it stains hands and tools.
choices.D: A 2022 trial found tomatoes in charcoal-amended sand needed fewer waterings.

hp-rw-es-16.explanation: Goal = production method only, no results. B is pure production. A mixes method with results; C/D ignore production.
hp-rw-es-16.method: Underline the goal constraints: how made + without results.
hp-rw-es-16.speedTip: Exclude any sentence that reports the tomato trial.
hp-rw-es-16.commonTrap: Including the helpful watering result when the goal forbids results.

hp-rw-es-17.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ada Lovelace wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine in the 1840s.
• Her notes include what many historians consider an early algorithm intended for machine processing.
• Babbage designed the engine but did not complete a full working version in his lifetime.
• Modern programming languages appeared more than a century later.

The student wants to challenge the idea that useful computing algorithms began only in the twentieth century. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Modern programming languages appeared more than a century after Lovelace's notes.
choices.B: Babbage designed the Analytical Engine but never finished a full working version.
choices.C: In the 1840s, Ada Lovelace wrote notes presenting what many historians view as an early machine-processing algorithm—well before twentieth-century programming languages.
choices.D: Charles Babbage worked on calculating machines in the nineteenth century.

hp-rw-es-17.explanation: Challenge requires early algorithm + pre-20th-century timing. C does both. A alone doesn't assert Lovelace's algorithm; B/D miss the algorithm point.
hp-rw-es-17.method: To challenge 'only 20th century,' show a clear earlier algorithm example.
hp-rw-es-17.commonTrap: Mentioning Babbage unfinished machine without the algorithm claim.

hp-rw-es-18.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Green roofs cover buildings with vegetation over a waterproof membrane.
• They can reduce stormwater runoff and lower rooftop temperatures.
• Installation costs are typically higher than for conventional roofs.
• A Chicago city hall green roof became a widely cited early municipal example in the U.S.

The student wants to present a drawback of green roofs. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

choices.D: Green roofs, which cover buildings with vegetation over a waterproof membrane, typically cost more to install than conventional roofs.
choices.A: Green roofs can reduce stormwater runoff and lower rooftop temperatures.
choices.B: Chicago's city hall green roof is a widely cited early municipal example in the U.S.
choices.C: Green roofs include a waterproof membrane beneath vegetation.

hp-rw-es-18.explanation: Drawback = higher installation cost. C states it (with brief definition OK). A is benefit; B is example; D is neutral structure.
hp-rw-es-18.speedTip: Scan notes for the negative bullet—costs higher.
hp-rw-es-18.commonTrap: Selecting benefits or famous examples when asked for a drawback.

hp-rw-es-19.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that rarely interact with matter.
• Enormous detectors are built underground to catch occasional neutrino interactions.
• The IceCube detector uses Antarctic ice as its detection medium.
• Neutrino astronomy can observe cosmic events that light-based telescopes miss when dust blocks light.

The student wants to explain why neutrino astronomy can complement light-based telescopes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes?

choices.A: Neutrinos rarely interact with matter, so enormous underground detectors are required.
choices.B: IceCube uses Antarctic ice as its detection medium.
choices.C: Because neutrinos can reveal cosmic events even when dust blocks light, neutrino astronomy can observe sources that light-based telescopes miss.

hp-rw-es-19.explanation: Complement = see what light telescopes miss when dust blocks. C. A/B/D are properties/detector facts without the complementarity.
hp-rw-es-19.method: Goal keyword complement → unique observational advantage vs light.
hp-rw-es-19.speedTip: Dust-blocking limitation of light → neutrino advantage.
hp-rw-es-19.commonTrap: Defining neutrinos or naming IceCube without the complementarity.

hp-rw-es-20.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Board game Go has more possible legal positions than atoms estimated in the observable universe (order-of-magnitude comparisons often cited in AI writing).
• In 2016, an AI system defeated a top human Go champion in a high-profile match.
• Earlier AI systems had long struggled with Go compared with chess.
• The victory intensified public debate about machine learning breakthroughs.

The student wants to note the 2016 result without mentioning chess or public debate. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

choices.A: In 2016, an AI system defeated a top human Go champion, renewing debate about machine learning.
choices.B: Earlier AI systems had long struggled with Go compared with chess, but a 2016 system won a high-profile match.
choices.C: In 2016, an AI system defeated a top human Go champion in a high-profile match.
choices.D: Go has more possible positions than atoms in the observable universe, which is why AI struggled compared with chess.

hp-rw-es-20.explanation: Constraints: include 2016 win; exclude chess and debate. Only C complies. A has debate; B/D have chess.
hp-rw-es-20.method: Check negative constraints first—eliminate any choice with forbidden topics.
hp-rw-es-20.speedTip: Forbidden words: chess, debate → cross out A/B/D.
hp-rw-es-20.commonTrap: Keeping a 'harmless' extra clause that violates the without-mentioning rule.

hp-rw-es-21.stem:
Passage: Many coastal towns tout seawalls as permanent protection. Yet seawalls can accelerate erosion on adjacent unprotected beaches by reflecting wave energy sideways—protecting one parcel while shifting risk next door.

The primary purpose of the second sentence is to

choices.A: provide a definition of wave energy.
choices.B: qualify the promise of seawalls by explaining a harmful side effect.
choices.C: argue that all coastal construction should stop.

hp-rw-es-21.explanation: Yet signals contrast; the sentence limits the 'permanent protection' claim with a spillover harm. B. A/D wrong focus; C too extreme.
hp-rw-es-21.method: Purpose of a Yet sentence = often qualify/complicate prior claim.
hp-rw-es-21.speedTip: Spot contrast word → look for qualify/limit among choices.
hp-rw-es-21.commonTrap: Reading a qualification as a call to ban all construction.

hp-rw-es-22.stem:
Passage: The biologist opens with a puzzling observation: desert beetles collect drinking water from fog on their bumps and grooves. She then walks through lab tests that isolate which surface features matter most, before closing with designs for fog-harvesting panels.

Which choice best describes the passage's overall structure?

choices.A: A chronological biography of the biologist.
choices.B: A problem-solution advertisement for a commercial product.
choices.C: An observation followed by experimental analysis and an applied implication.
choices.D: A debate between two competing theories of desert survival.

hp-rw-es-22.explanation: Observation → lab isolation → applied design matches C. Not a biography, ad, or two-theory debate.
hp-rw-es-22.method: Label each section's job, then match the arc.
hp-rw-es-22.speedTip: Observation → tests → application is a common science structure.
hp-rw-es-22.commonTrap: Forcing a debate structure when only one investigative line appears.

hp-rw-es-23.stem:
Passage: Critics call the mural merely decorative. That label undersells it: the panels sequence a neighborhood's labor history, inviting viewers to track how industries arrived, peaked, and left.

As used in the passage, undersells most nearly means

choices.A: advertises at too low a price.
choices.B: fails to convey the full importance of.

hp-rw-es-23.explanation: Context: 'merely decorative' is inadequate; undersells = doesn't convey full importance. Not literal price, lowering, or translation.
hp-rw-es-23.speedTip: Ignore marketplace literal meaning when figurative fits.

hp-rw-es-24.stem:
Passage: (1) Renewable energy advocates often highlight plunging solar panel costs. (2) Less often discussed is the bottleneck of transmission lines that must carry that power to cities. (3) Without grid upgrades, cheap panels alone cannot deliver on their promise.

The function of sentence 2 is primarily to

choices.A: introduce a neglected constraint that complicates the cost narrative.
choices.B: provide a statistical table of panel prices.
choices.C: concede that solar power cannot work anywhere.
choices.D: summarize the entire argument in one slogan.

hp-rw-es-24.explanation: Sentence 2 pivots to a less-discussed bottleneck (transmission), setting up sentence 3. A. No table; C is absolute; D is what sentence 3 partly does, not 2 alone.
hp-rw-es-24.method: Ask what new idea sentence 2 adds relative to sentence 1.
hp-rw-es-24.speedTip: Less often discussed = signal for neglected complication.
hp-rw-es-24.commonTrap: Treating a bottleneck mention as a total impossibility claim.

Math M1: linear / systems / % with Desmos on every system or graph
One timed module only (weaker side): hit pace checkpoints, mark at 90s
Log every miss same day — content vs misread vs trap vs time

Redo all misses cold before bed — same stem, new eyes

forecast.method: Digital SAT domain base rates × Module-1 unlock weight for a 600→1550 climber. ScoreEV is unlock-weighted expected points, not raw frequency. Adversarial merge of RW Examsmith position + Math domain priors; low-EV claims killed.
forecast.thesis: Module-1 unlock dominates residual EV. RW: Boundaries + Form/Structure + Transitions first; Evidence/Synthesis next; Craft last. Math: Algebra linear/systems + Advanced Math quadratics + PSDA ratios first; Geometry demoted as time-sink.

rwTypes.rationale: Highest Module-1 unlock EV. Comma splice vs period/semicolon and intro-clause commas are the #1 leak for ~600 RW. Binary traps; high trainability; near-certain appearance both modules.
rwTypes.dissent: Craft advocates claim purpose Qs matter more for 1550 ceiling — rejected for THIS student until Hard M2 is unlocked. Frequency ≠ unlock EV only after gate is secured.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Treating a comma as a legal joiner between two independent clauses.

rwTypes.rationale: S-V agreement with intervening phrases, tense consistency, modifiers, parallelism. Fast points once patterned. Direct M1 accuracy insurance.
rwTypes.dissent: Slightly less binary than Boundaries; still top-tier. Do not demote below Vocab.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Matching verb to nearest noun instead of true subject.

rwTypes.rationale: Contrast/cause/addition logic is extremely trainable and time-cheap. For a 600 student these are NOT already banked — Timing Coach claims of 'free points' are aspirational, not current.
rwTypes.dissent: Timing Coach may underrate residual miss rate under clock. Sprint Architect should still overweight early-week.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Picking a transition that fits local sentence tone but breaks paragraph logic.

rwTypes.rationale: Text+table/claim support is high-frequency. Extreme/unsupported claims kill Hard M2. ScoreEV solid AFTER conventions lock; slower per item than Transitions.
rwTypes.dissent: Raw frequency fans put this #2; Module-1 unlock weight keeps it behind conventions/transitions for a gate student.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Choosing a detail that is true in the passage but does not support the stated claim.

rwTypes.rationale: Goal-matching is highly trainable. Wrong-goal and off-register traps swing Hard M2. Pack with evidence, not before Boundaries.
rwTypes.dissent: Lower raw count than Words in Context — still higher scoreEV for 1550 because distractors are cleaner once goal is underlined.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Satisfying tone while missing the bullet-goal (e.g., compare vs introduce).

rwTypes.rationale: Near-certain appearance; precision > synonym hunting. High pAppear but LOWER Module-1 unlock EV than conventions because distractors feel 'almost right' under time.
rwTypes.dissent: KILLED as a primary unlock lever. Still drill lightly — do not build a vocab-only week.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Picking a synonym that fits dictionary meaning but not passage function.

rwTypes.rationale: Must appear; leaps and too-strong claims burn time. Medium priority behind evidence/synthesis.
rwTypes.dissent: KILLED as early-sprint priority. Overdrilling inferences before conventions is a classic 600→stuck pattern.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Selecting an answer that goes one logical step beyond the text.

rwTypes.rationale: Purpose/structure always shows; verbal load is high. Hard M2 polish, NOT the first unlock lever. Frequency without unlock weight = low EV for this student.
rwTypes.dissent: KILLED as Day-1 overweight. Reintroduce only after M1 conventions hit ≤2 miss target.
rwTypes.m1Trap: Confusing overall purpose with a local paragraph function.

mathTypes.rationale: Algebra dominates Digital SAT Math volume. Linear equations, inequalities, and 2-var systems are the Module-1 unlock core for ~600 Math. Desmos intersection is legal speed.
mathTypes.dissent: Advanced Math fans want quadratics first — rejected until linear/systems hit ≥90% timed accuracy.

mathTypes.rationale: PSDA percent/ratio/rate items are high-frequency and high-miss for 600 students. Unit slip and percent-of vs percent-change are classic M1 leaks.
mathTypes.dissent: Sometimes labeled 'easy' — empirically they are not for this baseline. Keep in M1 bank.

cards: Boundaries ≤35s: independent+independent → comma alone is illegal. Decide join type before choices.

Transitions ≤30s: label before/after as contrast|cause|addition — then pick. Tone-fit without logic = trap.

cards: Evidence: claim first (underline), then hunt proof — never read the whole stem hoping the answer appears.

Synthesis: 3-word goal rewrite before options; any choice missing one word dies immediately.
Hard mark 90s. One stuck evidence stem cascading into rushed conventions is how 600 students fail the unlock.

cards: Checkpoints Q7/Q14. Behind? Flag geo/trig and finish linear/% first — unlock > pride.
Percent: write (new−old)/old every time. Clock pressure invents 'of' vs 'change' errors.
Linear clean ≤60s by hand; if coeffs get messy, Desmos verify — don't re-expand.
Target ≤2 M1 misses. Finishing 3 min early with two careless % misses is a failed unlock.
speedCards.timeCostNote: Algebra/% are high scoreEV AND should be time-cheap. Geometry is low scoreEV and high timeCost — demote under clock.

cards: Two equations → graph both, read intersection. Algebra-first on systems is the #1 time leak for ~600 Math.
Nonlinear: y1/y2 graph + zoom before expanding. If picture is clear in 15s, stop algebra thrash.
Parallel/inconsistent: Desmos shows it instantly — don't prove by elimination under clock.
Last-8 rule: geo stalls get flagged; return only with leftover. Seconds-per-point > 'I almost had it'.
speedCards.timeCostNote: Desmos systems outrank Geometry on time-adjusted EV even when geo 'feels harder'. Method beats domain vanity.
